|18 |45-Degree Leg Press                      |"{\"grip\": \"\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the lower back and hips flat against the pad throughout the descent instead of allowing the pelvis to tuck under.\", \"setup\": \"Sit in the sled with the back and hips flat against the pad and feet placed shoulder-width on the platform.\", \"execution\": \"Lower the sled by bending the hips and knees until a controlled depth is reached, then press it back up through the feet without locking the knees aggressively.\", \"stop_when\": \"The lower back rounds off the pad or the sled can no longer be pressed back to the starting position.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet placed shoulder-width apart on the platform, positioned centrally or slightly toward the middle-to-upper portion of the plate depending on comfort, toes pointed slightly outward or straight ahead.\", \"bracing\": \"Lower back and hips pressed firmly into the pad throughout the movement, with abdominal bracing maintained to prevent the pelvis from tucking or the lower back from rounding off the pad at the bottom of the range.\", \"overview\": \"This is the 45-degree plate-loaded leg press, performed on an angled sled machine in which the lifter pushes the weighted platform away along a fixed linear track. The fixed sled path removes the balance and bracing demands of a free-standing squat while preserving a similar hip-and-knee-dominant flexion/extension pattern. It differs from a horizontal or vertical leg press primarily in the angle of the sled track, which affects trunk position and the relative demand on the hip versus knee extensors.\", \"eccentric\": \"The sled lowers under control back toward the body through hip and knee flexion, with the knees traveling toward the chest along the fixed sled path while the lower back remains in contact with the pad.\", \"concentric\": \"The sled is pressed away from the body through simultaneous hip and knee extension, with the feet driving evenly into the platform and the lower back remaining flat against the pad throughout.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Avoid bouncing the sled off the bottom stops or using the safety catches to generate rebound momentum; a controlled descent and press are expected throughout.\", \"end_position\": \"Legs extended with the knees not aggressively locked, sled at the top of its travel with the hips still flat against the pad.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Engage the safety catches or stops appropriately when racking or approaching technical failure.\", \"Avoid locking the knees explosively at the top of the range under heavy load.\", \"Keep the entire foot in contact with the platform to avoid unstable load distribution.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Press the platform up and away; keep the hips pinned to the pad throughout the movement.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Push the platform away using the whole foot; think of driving the knees away from the chest rather than just straightening the legs.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the lower back to round and lift off the pad at the bottom of the range.\", \"Locking the knees aggressively at the top of each repetition.\", \"Letting the knees cave inward during the press.\", \"Bouncing the sled off the safety stops or the bottom of the range to generate momentum.\", \"Placing the feet very low on the platform, causing the heels to lift off the plate.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"45-degree sled leg press machine with the seat back angle fixed by the machine design, safety catches or stops set appropriately, footplate positioned to allow full contact of the feet.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"From the top position with the legs extended to the point at which the hips can no longer flex further without the lower back rounding off the pad, defining the exercise-specific usable depth.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to press the sled back to the extended position while keeping the lower back against the pad, as distinct from continuing to move the sled by rounding the lower back off the pad.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Slower sled speed through the bottom portion of the range, minor but still acceptable inward knee drift, and increasing effort to keep the lower back against the pad, while the ROM and hip contact remain intact.\", \"individualization\": \"Foot placement height and width on the platform, and the depth of the descent, may vary moderately with limb proportions and hip mobility, provided the lower back remains against the pad throughout the range that is used.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane hip and knee flexion/extension, occurring along the fixed diagonal path of the sled.\", \"starting_position\": \"Seated with the lower back and hips flat against the pad, feet placed on the platform at a shoulder-width stance, knees tracking in line with the toes, sled unracked with the legs extended but knees not locked aggressively.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the lower back rounds and lifts off the pad during the descent, the knees cave inward under load, or the sled can no longer be pressed back to the extended position.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Combined hip extension and knee extension |9  |Pendlay Row                              |"{\"grip\": \"Pronated grip slightly wider than shoulder width, adjustable moderately based on torso length and shoulder comfort while keeping the pulling path directed toward the lower ribcage.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the torso angle fixed and parallel to the floor throughout the pull instead of rising toward vertical.\", \"setup\": \"Hinge at the hips until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor with the bar resting on the ground below the shoulders.\", \"execution\": \"Pull the bar explosively off the floor into the lower ribcage/upper abdomen, then return it fully to the floor and reset before each repetition.\", \"stop_when\": \"The torso angle rises noticeably to help lift the bar or the bar can no longer be pulled to the torso from a dead stop.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet roughly hip- to shoulder-width apart, positioned to allow the bar to travel in a straight vertical line without hitting the shins.\", \"bracing\": \"Abdominal bracing combined with a fixed neutral spine and locked hip hinge angle; the torso must not rise or the lower back round as the bar is pulled from the floor.\", \"overview\": \"This is the Pendlay row, a barbell row variant performed from a torso position held approximately parallel to the floor, in which the bar returns to and rests on the floor between every repetition rather than remaining suspended. Each repetition begins from a dead stop with the spine and hips in a fixed hinge position, distinguishing it from a bent-over row performed with continuous tension and a more upright torso, and from a chest-supported row in which the torso is externally braced.\", \"eccentric\": \"The bar is lowered under control back to the floor along the same vertical path, with the elbows extending and the shoulders returning to a neutral hang while the torso angle stays constant until the bar makes full contact with the floor.\", \"concentric\": \"The bar is pulled explosively from the floor toward the lower ribcage/upper abdomen through simultaneous glenohumeral extension and elbow flexion, with the torso angle and hip hinge remaining fixed throughout the pull.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"The concentric pull is typically performed with intent to move the bar quickly from the floor, while the bar is set down under control rather than dropped; a brief pause with the bar on the floor between repetitions is a defining feature of this variant.\", \"end_position\": \"Bar making light contact with the lower ribcage/upper abdomen with the elbows driven up and back and the shoulder blades retracted.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Maintain a neutral spine throughout the hinge position given the loaded flexed-hip posture.\", \"Ensure the bar path stays close to the shins and thighs without striking them during the pull.\", \"Use plates that keep the bar at a consistent floor height to avoid an inconsistent starting range.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Pull the bar into the lower ribs; keep the torso locked at the same angle relative to the floor throughout the set.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Pull the elbows back and up toward the ceiling while keeping the torso angle fixed; think of holding the hips and spine in the same position from the first pull to the last.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the torso to rise toward vertical during the pull, converting the movement into a more upright row.\", \"Rounding the lower back as the bar leaves the floor.\", \"Using momentum from a bouncing torso instead of a fixed hinge position.\", \"Shrugging the shoulders upward instead of driving the elbows back.\", \"Failing to return the bar fully to the floor between repetitions.\", \"Pulling the bar toward the mid-chest instead of the lower ribcage/upper abdomen.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Bar loaded on the floor, plates sized so the bar sits at a fixed, consistent height for each dead-stop repetition.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"From the bar resting fully on the floor at the bottom to contact with the lower ribcage at the top, with each repetition beginning from a true dead stop rather than a suspended position.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to pull the bar from the floor to the torso while maintaining the established torso angle and neutral spine, as distinct from moving the bar upward at all costs through torso extension or lumbar rounding.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Reduced bar speed off the floor, a longer pause before the bar clears the initial inches of travel, and increasing but still controlled effort to hold the torso angle, while the hinge position and pull path remain intact.\", \"individualization\": \"Torso angle, stance width, and grip width may vary moderately with limb proportions and hip mobility, provided the torso angle remains fixed throughout each repetition and the spine stays in a neutral, extended position rather than rounding under load.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane glenohumeral extension and elbow flexion, with the torso and hips held in a fixed sagittal-plane hinge that does not contribute movement to the pull itself.\", \"starting_position\": \"Feet positioned under the bar, hips hinged back with the torso angled to approximately parallel with the floor, spine held in a neutral, extended position, arms hanging vertically to grip the bar directly below the shoulders, bar resting on the floor.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the torso angle rises toward vertical to assist the pull, the lower back rounds or extends beyond its starting position, or the bar can no longer be pulled from the floor to the torso without a change in hip or spine position.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Glenohumeral extension combined with horizontal extension as the upper arm moves posteriorly toward the torso; elbow flexion driven by the biceps and brachialis; scapulae retract as the bar approaches the torso; the hips and spine remain in an isometric hinge position, with the erector spinae, glutes, and hamstrings acting as stabilizers rather than prime movers.\"}" |61 |Heavy Dumbbell Lateral Raise             |"{\"grip\": \"Neutral to lightly pronated, handles held centred in the palm with the wrists in line with the forearms. The wrist should not be actively cocked upward or allowed to collapse; the dumbbell stays approximately level rather than tipping so that one end leads the raise.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Any body English must be a small, controlled assist at the bottom only; the lift above the mid-range must still be produced by the shoulders.\", \"setup\": \"Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at the sides, feet hip-width, elbows in a slight fixed bend.\", \"execution\": \"Raise both dumbbells out to the sides to about shoulder height, permitting a small, deliberate torso and hip pulse to pass the hardest portion of the range.\", \"stop_when\": \"The dumbbells no longer reach approximately shoulder height, or the trunk swing becomes the primary mover rather than a small assist.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet approximately hip- to shoulder-width, weight through the whole foot, knees softly flexed and available for a small dip that initiates the assist.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain abdominal tension sufficient to keep the ribcage from flaring and the lumbar spine from hyperextending during the trunk pulse, so the body English occurs as a small, controlled hip and trunk cycle rather than a lumbar arch. Light glute engagement anchors the pelvis. The scapulae stay set and depressed at the start of the ascent so the assist does not become a shrug.\", \"overview\": \"A standing bilateral shoulder-abduction exercise performed with a load heavier than a strict lateral raise permits, in which a limited amount of trunk and hip movement is accepted to carry the dumbbells through the portion of the range where the deltoid's leverage is poorest. This is deliberately distinct from the strict standing variant, in which the torso is held rigidly upright and no body movement is tolerated, and from the forward-leaning variant, in which a static torso lean is used to align the resistance more favourably with the line of lateral deltoid pull. Here the torso begins approximately upright and a small, controlled hip and trunk pulse initiates the ascent, after which the shoulders complete and control the rest of the range. The permitted body English is a bounded technical feature, not an absence of standards: the eccentric remains fully controlled by the shoulders and the top position is still reached by abduction rather than by momentum alone.\", \"eccentric\": \"Lower both dumbbells under shoulder control along the same arc back to the sides, with no assistance from the trunk and no free-fall. The torso is upright and stationary during the descent; hip and knee movement occurs only at the transition into the next repetition. The scapulae downwardly rotate under control and the shoulders do not roll forward at the bottom.\", \"concentric\": \"Initiate with a small, controlled dip and drive through the knees and hips, timed so the resulting momentum carries the dumbbells through the lower and early mid-range where the deltoid moment arm is least favourable. As the arms pass roughly 45 degrees of abduction, the trunk returns to its starting alignment and the shoulders complete the raise to approximately shoulder height. The dumbbells travel outward and slightly forward of the frontal plane, the elbow angle stays fixed, and the arms rise as units with the elbows leading marginally ahead of the hands. The dumbbells should not be flung; the upper half of the range must be under active shoulder control.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"The assist is a single, timed dip and drive at the initiation of the ascent, not a continuous rhythmic bounce across repetitions. The eccentric is deliberately controlled at normal speed, since it is the phase in which the shoulder handles the load without assistance.\", \"end_position\": \"Upper arms at approximately shoulder height in or slightly forward of the frontal plane, elbows still in their fixed bend, shoulders not shrugged toward the ears, torso returned to its starting alignment.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Keep the trunk pulse a hip and knee action; repeated lumbar hyperextension under an anteriorly displaced load is the main injury-relevant pattern here.\", \"Terminate the set when the eccentric can no longer be controlled by the shoulders, since uncontrolled descent from shoulder height loads the glenohumeral joint in abduction.\", \"Set the dumbbells down by hinging at the hips with a neutral spine rather than releasing them from the hanging position.\", \"Keep the arms in or slightly forward of the scapular plane rather than forcing them behind it during the assisted portion.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Push the dumbbells out and away to shoulder height rather than up; stop the dumbbells cleanly at the top instead of letting them travel on.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Time one small knee and hip drive to the start of the raise, then finish with the shoulders; keep the shoulders down as the arms rise; lower with the shoulders alone.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Letting the trunk swing through a large flexion-extension arc so momentum, rather than the shoulders, carries the arms through the entire range.\", \"Hyperextending the lumbar spine during the drive instead of keeping the ribcage stacked over the pelvis.\", \"Dropping the dumbbells on the descent rather than lowering them under shoulder control.\", \"Shrugging the shoulders so the arms are elevated by scapular elevation rather than glenohumeral abduction.\", \"Progressively opening the elbow angle during the set to shorten the resistance lever.\", \"Continuing the raise well above shoulder height on the momentum of the assist.\", \"Turning the assist into a continuous bounce so each repetition begins before the previous one has been controlled.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"\", \"range_of_motion\": \"From the arms hanging at the sides to approximately shoulder height, where scapular upward rotation begins to dominate over glenohumeral abduction. The permitted body English exists to complete this range under heavier load, not to extend it; raising the dumbbells above shoulder height with a larger swing is outside the intended ROM. At the bottom, the arms return to the sides between repetitions rather than stopping at a partial position.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"RIR 0 is the last repetition in which the dumbbells reach approximately shoulder height with the upper half of the range produced by shoulder abduction after a small assist, and with a controlled eccentric. Further repetitions may still be possible using a full-body swing, a pronounced shrug, or a partial raise with a dropped descent, but those no longer represent this exercise.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"The dumbbells decelerate markedly in the upper third of the range and the top position becomes harder to hold cleanly. The assist naturally becomes slightly larger while remaining a discrete pulse rather than a swing, and terminal height may sit fractionally lower, while the eccentric is still shoulder-controlled and the arms still reach approximately shoulder height. Grip and upper-trapezius tension typically become noticeable. These signs are consistent with roughly one technically valid repetition remaining, though the estimate is imprecise and less sharply defined here than in the strict variant.\", \"individualization\": \"The magnitude of permitted body English varies with the load used and with individual trunk control; the defining constraint is that it remains a discrete, timed assist through the low mid-range with the upper portion and the entire eccentric under shoulder control. The arm path may sit anywhere from the frontal plane to roughly 20-30 degrees forward of it depending on scapular orientation and shoulder comfort. Fixed elbow angle may range from nearly straight to about 30 degrees of flexion provided it does not change within a set. Terminal height varies slightly with shoulder structure; stopping just below shoulder level is legitimate where scapular elevation would otherwise dominate. Stance width, degree of knee softening, and grip orientation are matters of preference. A small controlled assist is the defining feature of this variant, not a fault; an uncontrolled full-body swing is a technical error, and holding a rigidly static torso throughout constitutes the strict variant rather than this one.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily frontal- and scapular-plane shoulder abduction, with the arms typically travelling slightly forward of the pure frontal plane; a small sagittal-plane hip and trunk component is deliberately permitted at the initiation of the ascent.\", \"starting_position\": \"Standing tall with the dumbbells hanging at or just in front of the thighs, palms facing the body or slightly rotated inward. Elbows in a slight fixed bend of roughly 10-20 degrees. Torso approximately vertical or with a very small forward inclination, ribcage stacked over the pelvis, pelvis neutral, shoulders set down rather than shrugged. Knees softly unlocked so a small dip and drive is available.\", \"technical_failure\": \"Failure occurs when the shoulders can no longer complete the upper half of the range after the assist, or when the assist grows beyond a small controlled pulse. Observable breakdowns include the dumbbells failing to reach approximately shoulder height, the trunk swinging through a large flexion-extension arc so momentum carries the arms through the whole range, the lumbar spine hyperextending as the arms rise, the shoulders shrugging so the trapezius elevates the arms, elbow angle progressively increasing to shorten the lever, the eccentric being dropped rather than lowered, or the arms rising asymmetrically with one side jerked up.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Glenohumeral abduction in or near the scapular plane, accompanied by scapular upward rotation as the arms approach shoulder height. The elbow holds a fixed slight flexion angle and the radioulnar joints hold a static pronated-to-neutral position. The hips and lumbar spine perform a small, controlled extension-flexion cycle at the start of each repetition rather than remaining purely isometric; the abdominal wall and erector spinae control that motion and return the trunk to its starting alignment.\"}"|
|142|Single-Leg Calf Raise                    |"{\"grip\": \"\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Drive straight upward through the big toe and second toe without letting the ankle roll inward or outward.\", \"setup\": \"Stand on one leg on a flat, stable surface with light fingertip support on a wall or rack for balance only.\", \"execution\": \"Rise onto the ball of the foot as high as possible, then lower under control until the heel lightly touches the floor.\", \"stop_when\": \"You can no longer reach full plantarflexion at the top or the ankle begins to wobble laterally to complete the rep.\"}, \"stance\": \"Single-leg stance on the working foot, foot pointing forward or very slightly turned out, positioned directly under the hip.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain a level pelvis and stacked ribcage-pelvis alignment to prevent trunk lean toward the working leg; keep the standing knee position constant rather than allowing it to buckle inward or hyperextend as balance is challenged.\", \"overview\": \"This is a single-leg, bodyweight-only calf raise performed on a flat surface rather than an elevated edge or platform, which limits the eccentric range to the floor rather than a stretched position below neutral. It isolates unilateral plantarflexion strength and ankle-hip balance control, with the non-working leg lifted clear of the ground throughout. Because only bodyweight is used and no deficit is present, the exercise is primarily limited by ankle strength and single-leg balance rather than external load.\", \"eccentric\": \"Lower under control by allowing the ankle to dorsiflex, tracking the same vertical path as the ascent, until the heel makes light contact with the floor without collapsing suddenly under bodyweight.\", \"concentric\": \"Push through the ball of the foot to rise as high as possible into ankle plantarflexion, keeping the knee position fixed so the movement occurs at the ankle rather than through knee flexion or hip hike.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Lower with control rather than dropping the heel; a brief pause at the top may help confirm balance before descending, but no forced tempo is required.\", \"end_position\": \"Full plantarflexion with the heel at its highest point and weight balanced over the first and second metatarsal heads.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Keep a wall or rack within reach given the single-leg balance demand.\", \"Avoid performing on an unstable or compliant surface that could cause ankle inversion.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Rise straight up as if trying to touch the ceiling with the top of the head; keep the ankle tracking in a straight vertical line.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Push the floor away through the big toe; keep the hip level rather than hiking it to assist the rise.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Using the support hand to assist the lift rather than only for balance.\", \"Allowing the hip to hike or the torso to lean toward the working leg to help lift the heel.\", \"Bending the knee during the ascent to substitute knee extension for ankle plantarflexion.\", \"Dropping rapidly into the bottom position instead of controlling the descent.\", \"Letting the ankle roll inward or outward as fatigue increases.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"No equipment is required beyond a flat, non-compliant floor surface; a wall, pole, or rack may be used for one or two fingertips of light balance support only.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"From heel lightly touching the floor (full dorsiflexion available at neutral standing) to maximal active plantarflexion at the top; ROM is limited by ankle mobility and balance rather than by an elevated edge.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Failure to rise to a technically acceptable plantarflexion height using only the ankle, or requiring meaningful pulling/pushing force through the support hand to complete the repetition.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Noticeably slower rise, increased ankle wobble that is still self-corrected, and a smaller but still acceptable peak height compared to earlier repetitions.\", \"individualization\": \"The degree of forward foot lean, exact foot angle, and amount of fingertip support needed will vary with ankle mobility and balance ability; some lifters may naturally use a very slight forefoot turnout, provided the knee and hip remain stable and the movement stays isolated to the ankle.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane ankle plantarflexion, with continuous frontal- and transverse-plane stabilization demands at the hip and ankle to control single-leg balance.\", \"starting_position\": \"Stand on one leg with the knee softly extended (not locked), pelvis level, torso upright, and the non-working leg lifted with the hip and knee flexed so the foot clears the floor. The working foot points forward with weight distributed across the ball of the foot and heel resting on the ground.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The lifter can no longer reach a comparable peak plantarflexion height, needs to grip the wall for active assistance rather than balance, or the ankle repeatedly rolls medially/laterally to complete the rep.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Ankle plantarflexion at the talocrural joint through concentric and eccentric ranges; the standing hip and knee remain in a fixed, slightly flexed or extended position acting as stabilizers rather than prime movers; the contralateral hip flexes to clear the non-working leg.\"}" |68 |Close-Grip Seated Cable Row              |"{\"grip\": \"Neutral, palms facing each other, hands roughly 15-25 cm apart on the parallel handles. Wrists held in line with the forearms so the handle does not roll into flexion; grip firm enough to keep the wrist neutral without actively curling the handle toward the body.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Let the shoulders reach forward at the front of each repetition, then drive the elbows past the ribs rather than squeezing the handle to the body.\", \"setup\": \"Seated facing the low pulley, feet braced on the platform, torso close to vertical, holding a close neutral-grip V-handle.\", \"execution\": \"Pull the handle toward the lower ribs by driving the elbows back close to the torso while the trunk stays still.\", \"stop_when\": \"The handle can no longer reach the lower ribs without swinging the torso backward or shrugging the shoulders.\"}, \"stance\": \"Seated with both feet planted on the platform approximately hip-width apart, heels and forefeet in contact, legs used as a static brace rather than a driving segment.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain abdominal and oblique tension sufficient to keep the ribcage stacked over the pelvis so the torso angle does not change between the front and back of the stroke. Press the feet into the platform to anchor the pelvis on the seat, keep the lumbar spine neutral rather than allowing it to flex forward at the start or extend at the finish, and let the scapulae move on a stationary ribcage.\", \"overview\": \"A seated horizontal row performed on a low cable pulley with a close neutral grip, hands roughly 15-25 cm apart on a V-handle or similar close parallel-grip attachment. The neutral, narrow hand position keeps the humeri close to the torso through the pull, producing a shoulder extension-dominant path with substantial elbow flexor contribution, rather than the wider horizontal abduction path of a wide pronated row. The pull terminates at the lower ribs or upper abdomen rather than at the sternum, which distinguishes it from a chest-height row aimed more at the scapular retractors and posterior deltoid. Torso angle is held near vertical and constant; the trunk is not used as a rowing lever.\", \"eccentric\": \"Reverse the path by allowing the elbows to extend forward and the scapulae to protract and reach toward the pulley, under control and against continuous cable tension. The torso stays at the same angle rather than being pulled forward into flexion; the lumbar spine does not round as the arms extend. Trajectory mirrors the concentric.\", \"concentric\": \"Begin by drawing the shoulder blades back and slightly down as the humeri start to extend, then continue by driving the elbows rearward along a path close to the torso, forearms staying in line with the cable. The handle travels roughly horizontally toward the lower ribs or upper abdomen. Elbows finish behind the plane of the torso with the upper arms near the sides. The torso angle, knee angle, and neck position remain unchanged; the shoulders do not rise toward the ears.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Maintain continuous cable tension at the front of the stroke rather than letting the stack rebound. It differs from a Pendlay row, where the bar is reset on the floor between repetitions from a horizontal torso, and from a chest-supported row, where the postural demand is removed.\", \"eccentric\": \"Lower the bar under control along the same path until the arms are nearly straight and the scapulae are allowed to protract slightly, without the torso being pulled downward into spinal flexion or the hips rising to compensate. The hinge position is maintained continuously; the bar does not touch down between repetitions in this variant.\", \"concentric\": \"Initiate by drawing the shoulder blades back and slightly down as the humeri begin to extend, then pull the bar upward and slightly backward toward the lower ribs or upper abdomen with the elbows travelling behind the plane of the torso. The bar path is close to vertical relative to the floor and tracks near the thighs and abdomen rather than swinging forward. The torso angle, hip angle, and knee angle remain unchanged; the shoulders do not shrug toward the ears.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Each repetition should begin from a stationary torso rather than a hip or torso rebound; avoid a downward dip of the chest followed by an upward jerk. Continuous tension is maintained at the bottom rather than resting the bar on the floor.\", \"end_position\": \"Bar in contact with or immediately below the lower ribs or upper abdomen, elbows behind the torso, scapulae retracted, torso angle and hip angle identical to the starting position.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Set the hinge position and brace before lifting the bar off the floor, and reverse the same hinge to set it down rather than dropping it from the hanging position.\", \"Terminate the set when spinal neutrality can no longer be maintained, since the unsupported torso position makes lumbar flexion under load the primary risk.\", \"Hold the brace through each repetition rather than exhaling fully at the bottom of the range.\", \"Keep the cervical spine neutral rather than extending the neck to track the bar.\", \"Ensure sufficient clearance in front so the bar does not contact a rack or bench during the pull.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Pull the bar into the lower abdomen; keep the bar close to the thighs on the way up; push the floor away with the whole foot to stay anchored.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Drive the elbows back past the ribs; hold the hip angle fixed and pull only with the arms and shoulder blades; keep the ribcage stacked so the lower back neither rounds nor arches.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Raising the torso toward vertical during the pull so the hip extensors contribute to moving the bar.\", \"Dipping the chest downward and rebounding to start each repetition.\", \"Allowing the lumbar spine to round as the arms extend at the bottom.\", \"Pulling the bar toward the sternum with high elbows instead of to the lower ribs or abdomen.\", \"Letting the bar drift forward away from the thighs, increasing the moment on the lumbar spine.\", \"Extending the knees to add drive to the pull.\", \"Shrugging the shoulders toward the ears at the finish rather than retracting with the shoulders down.\", \"Hyperextending the cervical spine to look forward at a mirror.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Load the bar so it can be lifted from the floor or a rack to the hinged starting position without altering technique; Pulling the bar higher toward the sternum belongs to a different bar path and is not extra range here.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"RIR 0 is the last repetition completed with the bar reaching the lower ribs or upper abdomen, the elbows travelling behind the torso, a neutral spine, and a constant torso angle. Additional repetitions may still be possible using a torso swing, hip extension, or a partial pull, but those fall outside the technical standard for this variant and, unlike in a supported row, also represent the point at which spinal position is most likely to be compromised.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Bar velocity drops noticeably in the upper half of the pull and the top position becomes harder to reach. Small acceptable drift may appear as a few degrees of torso rise during the hardest repetitions or slightly reduced terminal elbow travel, while spinal neutrality, bar contact height, and full bottom extension are still preserved. Grip and erector fatigue commonly become noticeable. These signs suggest approximately one technically valid repetition remains, though the judgement is inherently approximate given the postural demand.\", \"individualization\": \"Torso angle may legitimately sit anywhere from roughly 30 to 60 degrees above horizontal depending on hip mobility, hamstring length, spinal comfort, and the emphasis chosen for the pull; flatter torso angles increase the postural demand and shift bar contact lower, more upright angles reduce it. Elbow path may range from close to the torso to moderately flared, which changes bar contact height accordingly. Knee flexion, stance width, and use of straps or a hook grip are matters of preference. |64 |Cable Rear-Delt Fly                      |"{\"grip\": \"Neutral to semi-pronated on a single handle, wrist held in line with the forearm so the handle does not roll into flexion or extension under load. distinct from continuing to move the dumbbell by lifting the upper arm off the pad.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Reduced curl height, slower concentric speed, and a growing tendency for the upper arm to lift slightly off the pad, while the general path remains intact.\", \"individualization\": \"Pad height and torso position relative to the bench may vary moderately with limb length and shoulder comfort, provided the upper arm remains against the pad throughout the curl and the forearm stays in a neutral rotation.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Sagittal-plane elbow flexion and extension, with the shoulder fixed in a supported flexed position throughout.\", \"starting_position\": \"Seated or standing at the preacher bench with the working upper arm flat against the pad, elbow extended, dumbbell held with a neutral grip, opposite hand may brace on the bench or opposite knee for stability.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the dumbbell can no longer be curled without the |76 |Low-Bar Back Squat                       |"{\"grip\": \"Use a pronated grip outside the shoulders at a width that permits a secure posterior-deltoid shelf without painful shoulder, elbow, or wrist positioning. Maintain upper-back tension and keep the wrists as neutral as practical; the hands secure the bar against the back rather than carrying its load.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Maintain the low-bar shelf and keep the bar balanced over the midfoot despite the greater forward torso inclination.\", \"setup\": \"Place the bar across the posterior deltoids below the upper trapezius, create a rigid upper-back shelf, and stand with the whole foot planted in a stance that permits the knees and hips to track freely.\", \"execution\": \"Descend by sitting the hips back and down with coordinated knee flexion, then drive the hips and shoulders upward together while keeping the bar vertically over the midfoot.\", \"stop_when\": \"Stop when another repetition would require major spinal flexion, loss of the bar shelf, pronounced hip shoot, marked knee collapse, or a materially shortened depth.\"}, \"stance\": \"Use a stance generally around shoulder width or moderately wider, with the toes turned outward according to hip anatomy and comfort. Maintain pressure through the heel and both sides of the forefoot while allowing the knees to track in the same general direction as the toes.\", \"bracing\": \"Create strong circumferential abdominal pressure before descending and preserve a rigid relationship between the ribcage and pelvis. Maintain spinal extensor tension and the upper-back contraction required to keep the bar fixed on the posterior-deltoid shelf. Resist uncontrolled lumbar flexion, pelvic rotation, and lateral trunk shift throughout the repetition.\", \"overview\": \"A barbell back squat performed with the bar positioned low across the posterior deltoids, below the upper trapezius. Compared with the high-bar variant, the low-bar position requires greater forward torso inclination and generally produces a more hip-dominant squat pattern while still involving substantial knee extension. The defining mechanics are a secure posterior-shoulder bar shelf, coordinated hip and knee motion, and a bar path maintained vertically over the midfoot.\", \"eccentric\": \"Descend under control by flexing the hips and knees together, allowing the hips to travel backward as the torso inclines forward sufficiently to keep the low-positioned bar over the midfoot. Maintain whole-foot pressure, stable knee tracking, a rigid trunk, and a secure bar shelf until the intended depth is reached.\", \"concentric\": \"Drive through the whole foot and extend the hips and knees together while keeping the bar vertically over the midfoot. Maintain the forward torso inclination required by the low-bar position without allowing the hips to rise markedly faster than the shoulders. Keep the knees tracking with the toes and continue until the hips and knees return to a stable standing position.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Avoid uncontrolled free-fall into the bottom position or excessive rebound that disrupts the bar path. A natural stretch-shortening transition is acceptable if trunk rigidity, balance, and lower-limb alignment remain controlled.\", \"end_position\": \"The concentric ends standing with the hips and knees fully or nearly fully extended, the bar securely supported across the posterior deltoids, the trunk controlled, and the bar vertically aligned over the midfoot.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Set rack safeties below the intended bottom position so a failed repetition can be abandoned safely.\", \"Rest the bar on the posterior shoulder musculature rather than directly on the cervical or thoracic spinous processes.\", \"Do not force the shoulders into a grip width or degree of external rotation that causes pain solely to achieve a narrower hand position.\", \"Ensure the bar remains securely seated on the back before stepping away from the rack.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Keep the bar traveling straight down and up over the middle of your feet, and push the floor away as you stand.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Keep the upper back tight around the bar; stay balanced through the whole foot; drive the hips and shoulders upward together.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Placing the bar on the upper trapezius and unintentionally performing a high-bar squat.\", \"Failing to create a stable posterior-deltoid shelf and allowing the bar to slide down the back.\", \"Allowing the hips to rise substantially faster than the shoulders during the ascent.\", \"Trying to maintain an artificially upright torso and thereby shifting the bar away from the midfoot.\", \"Allowing the knees to collapse markedly inward relative to the feet.\", \"Losing heel or forefoot contact as balance shifts during the descent or ascent.\", \"Supporting excessive bar weight through extended wrists rather than maintaining the bar against the back with upper-back tension.\", \"Descending beyond controllable hip or spinal range and losing pelvic or lumbar position.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Set the rack hooks slightly below the height of the low-bar position so the bar can be unracked without excessive calf raise or trunk movement. Position safety pins or straps just below the intended bottom position so they do not interfere with normal range of motion but can receive the bar during a failed repetition.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"Descend to the greatest controlled depth that preserves whole-foot contact, knee tracking, spinal control, and the low-bar shelf. A typical competition-style low-bar squat reaches at least approximately the point where the hip crease is level with or below the top of the knee, but the usable depth should be limited by the ability to maintain the intended mechanics rather than forced through loss of pelvic or spinal control.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"RIR 0 is reached when no additional repetition can be completed from the prescribed depth to standing while maintaining the low-bar squat standard, even if the bar could still be raised by substantially shortening depth, allowing the chest to collapse, letting the hips shoot upward, losing the bar position, or shifting markedly away from midfoot balance.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Approximately one technically valid repetition may remain when ascent speed slows substantially through the sticking region and effort is visibly high, but the lifter can still preserve the low-bar shelf, intended depth, whole-foot balance, knee tracking, trunk rigidity, and bar path with only minor technical drift.\", \"individualization\": \"Stance width, toe angle, grip width, torso inclination, knee travel, hip depth, and exact bar placement may vary with femur length, tibial length, torso length, shoulder mobility, hip structure, and ankle dorsiflexion. Some lifters require a wider grip or slightly higher position within the low-bar region to maintain shoulder comfort, while others can place the bar lower across the posterior deltoids. The defining constraints are that the bar remains clearly below the high-bar trapezius position, stays securely supported by the posterior shoulder shelf, and travels vertically over the midfoot through coordinated hip and knee motion.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane hip, knee, and ankle motion, with substantial isometric trunk stabilization and frontal- and transverse-plane control of the pelvis, knees, feet, and shoulder girdle.\", \"starting_position\": \"Place the bar across the posterior deltoids and muscular tissue below the upper trapezius, not on the cervical spine. Retract and stabilize the shoulder girdle enough to create a firm shelf, then unrack and establish a stable stance with the entire foot supported. Keep the trunk rigid, head approximately neutral, and the bar vertically balanced over the midfoot before beginning the descent.\", \"technical_failure\": \"Technical failure occurs when another repetition cannot be completed through the intended depth without a material breakdown such as loss or migration of the low-bar shelf, substantial lumbar or thoracic flexion, the hips shooting upward while the chest collapses, loss of heel or forefoot contact, marked knee valgus, significant lateral shift, uncontrolled forward or backward bar displacement, or a substantial reduction in squat depth.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Concentric hip extension and knee extension with ankle plantarflexion from the dorsiflexed bottom position. The spinal extensors and abdominal wall stabilize the trunk substantially isometrically, while the shoulder girdle and upper back maintain the low-bar shelf and the hips stabilize the lower limbs against frontal- and transverse-plane deviation.\"}"                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
|4  |Dumbbell Overhead Press                  |"{\"grip\": \"Use a neutral-to-pronated grip that allows the wrists to remain stacked over the forearms. A slightly inward-facing hand position is acceptable and often permits a more natural scapular-plane arm path than forcing the palms fully forward.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Let the arms travel in the scapular plane and keep the wrists stacked over the elbows rather than forcing the dumbbells into a rigidly straight path.\", \"setup\": \"Sit against a near-upright backrest with the dumbbells at shoulder level, forearms approximately vertical, and feet firmly planted.\", \"execution\": \"Press the dumbbells upward by extending the elbows and elevating the upper arms while keeping the torso stable against the bench.\", \"stop_when\": \"Stop when another repetition would require excessive lumbar extension, major elbow-path deviation, shoulder shrugging beyond normal upward rotation, or a materially shortened range.\"}, \"stance\": \"Sit with both feet planted firmly at a comfortable width to stabilize the pelvis and prevent lower-body shifting during the press.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain abdominal and gluteal tension sufficient to keep the pelvis stable and prevent excessive lumbar extension or rib flare. The dumbbells begin near shoulder level and are pressed overhead through coordinated glenohumeral elevation and elbow extension. The usable bottom depth may vary with shoulder anatomy and mobility; forced deep shoulder extension or loss of control is not required.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"RIR 0 is reached when no additional repetition can be completed through the defined range with stable torso position and coordinated overhead arm mechanics, even if the dumbbells could still be moved by excessive spinal extension, major elbow-path changes, asymmetric leaning, or shortening the range.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Approximately one technically valid repetition may remain when pressing velocity slows substantially and the final portion becomes difficult, but both arms can still maintain comparable paths, stable wrist-elbow alignment, full intended range, and controlled torso position.\", \"individualization\": \"Backrest angle, elbow position, grip rotation, bottom depth, and the amount of inward dumbbell convergence may vary with shoulder structure, humeral length, thoracic mobility, and individual comfort. |1  |Bench Press                              |"{\"grip\": \"Use a closed pronated grip with the thumbs wrapped around the bar. Grip width may vary, but in the bottom position the forearms should remain approximately vertical when viewed from the front, with the wrists stacked reasonably over the elbows rather than markedly bent backward or inward.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the forearms approximately vertical near the bottom and maintain the same bar path on every repetition.\", \"setup\": \"Lie on the flat bench with stable upper-back contact, feet planted, and the bar positioned over the shoulder line.\", \"execution\": \"Lower the bar under control toward the lower-to-mid chest, then press it back up while keeping the torso and shoulder girdle stable.\", \"stop_when\": \"Stop when another repetition would require loss of the prescribed bar path, major shoulder-position change, bouncing, or substantial torso assistance.\"}, \"stance\": \"Place both feet firmly on the floor or another stable permitted support, far enough back to create whole-body stability without forcing the pelvis off the bench. Keep the ribcage and pelvis position stable, maintain pressure through the feet, and avoid shifting the torso, lifting the pelvis, or rotating during the repetition.\", \"overview\": \"A flat barbell bench press performed supine on a horizontal bench with a pronated bilateral grip. The defining movement is a controlled bar descent toward the lower-to-mid chest followed by a press back toward the shoulder line, using glenohumeral horizontal adduction and elbow extension while maintaining a stable torso and shoulder base. A moderate thoracic arch and scapular retraction are compatible with the variant, but the exercise should not become an exaggerated bridge or decline-style press.\", \"eccentric\": \"Lower the bar under active control from above the shoulder line downward and slightly forward toward the lower-to-mid chest. Press to full functional elbow extension without deliberately protracting the shoulders or losing the established bench position. If chest contact requires painful or unstable shoulder motion, use the greatest pain-free range that preserves the exercise mechanics.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"RIR 0 is reached when no additional repetition can be completed through the prescribed range while preserving the defined bench position, bar path, and joint alignment, even if the bar could still be moved using bouncing, excessive bridging, major elbow-path alteration, or other compensatory mechanics.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Approximately one technically valid repetition may remain when bar speed has slowed substantially and effort is high, but the lifter can still maintain the established touch point, bar path, torso position, wrist-elbow alignment, and full intended range without a major compensatory strategy.\", \"individualization\": \"Grip width, elbow angle, exact chest touch point, foot position, and degree of thoracic arch may vary with humeral length, shoulder anatomy, torso dimensions, mobility, and competition-style preferences. Unrack the bar to a position approximately above the shoulder joints with the elbows extended but not aggressively hyperextended.\", \"technical_failure\": \"Technical failure occurs when another repetition.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"During the concentric phase, the glenohumeral joints perform horizontal adduction with a small flexion component, the elbows extend, and the scapulae remain |77 |Smith Machine Split Squat                |"{\"grip\": \"Use a secure pronated grip on the Smith bar outside the shoulders, wide enough to maintain a stable upper-back position without forcing uncomfortable shoulder rotation. The hands stabilize the bar but should not pull or push against it to assist the repetition.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the front foot fully planted and let the front knee track naturally over the toes while the pelvis stays square.\", \"setup\": \"Stand under the Smith bar in a split stance with both feet on the floor, the front foot far enough forward to allow a deep descent without losing full-foot pressure.\", \"execution\": \"Lower the pelvis mostly straight down by flexing the front hip and knee while the rear knee descends toward the floor, then drive through the front leg to return to standing.\", \"stop_when\": \"Stop when another repetition would require pushing substantially from the rear leg, losing front-foot pressure, collapsing the front knee inward, or changing the established torso and pelvis position.\"}, \"stance\": \"Use a front-to-back split stance with both feet remaining on the floor. |107|Weighted Standing Ab Wheel Rollout       |"{\"grip\": \"Pronated grip on both handles, wrists held neutral and firm to prevent the loaded wheel from rotating uncontrollably in the hands.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Prevent the lumbar spine from sagging into extension at any point of the roll-out.\", \"setup\": \"Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, wheel loaded with plates on its axle positioned on the floor directly under the shoulders.\", \"execution\": \"Hinge at the hips and roll the wheel forward into a near-horizontal extended body position, then pull it back and rise to standing using abdominal and lat contraction rather than hip drive.\", \"stop_when\": \"The lumbar spine loses neutral position or the wheel cannot be reversed back to standing without dropping to the knees or hyperextending.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet hip-width apart, flat and stable on the floor, weight shifting toward the mid/forefoot as the hips move backward during the roll-out.\", \"bracing\": \"Maximal anterior abdominal bracing is required continuously to prevent lumbar hyperextension as the lever arm lengthens; obliques resist lateral shift or rotation of the trunk relative to the wheel's path; glutes provide minor control over hip position but must not substitute for abdominal bracing.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standing variant of the ab wheel rollout, initiated and completed from an upright standing position via a hip hinge rather than from a kneeling base, which substantially lengthens the lever arm and increases anti-extension demand on the trunk. The plate-weighted aspect adds external resistance loaded directly onto the wheel axle, increasing the destabilizing torque that the anterior core, obliques, and lats must resist throughout both the roll-out and the pull-back. It is mechanically distinct from the kneeling ab wheel rollout, which limits the lever arm and removes the hip-hinge and standing-return components entirely.\", \"eccentric\": \"The roll-out phase is the lengthening action: from standing, the hips hinge back and the shoulders flex as the wheel is allowed to travel forward under control, the torso progressively extending toward a near-horizontal position while the anterior core actively resists spinal extension rather than allowing the wheel's momentum to dictate the descent.\", \"concentric\": \"The pull-back phase is concentric: the wheel is dragged back toward the feet through combined shoulder extension and lat/abdominal contraction, the hips drive from a flexed hinge back toward extension, and the trunk transitions from the extended position back to standing while the spine is actively held in a neutral, non-extended posture.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Movement should remain continuous and controlled through both the roll-out and pull-back with no bouncing or rebounding off end-range tension, and no use of momentum to initiate the pull-back.\", \"end_position\": \"At full extension the torso is near-parallel to the floor, the arms are extended overhead in line with the torso, the hips are extended, the knees show only slight flexion, and the spine remains neutral without lumbar sag; this position marks the deepest point of the roll-out before reversal.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Plates loaded onto the axle must be secured with collars to prevent lateral shifting or sliding during the roll-out.\", \"Perform on a stable, non-slip surface with sufficient clear space in front of the lifter to accommodate full extension without obstruction.\", \"Attempting the fully standing version with heavy axle loading without established control in less demanding rollout variants can result in uncontrolled lumbar hyperextension if the pull-back fails at end-range.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Drive the wheel back toward the feet along the same line it rolled out on; keep the wheel's path close to a straight line extending directly forward from the starting point.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Brace the abdomen firmly before allowing the wheel to move; pull the body back toward the wheel using abdominal and lat contraction rather than yanking with the arms; keep the ribcage drawn down to avoid lower-back sagging.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the lumbar spine to sag into extension during the roll-out instead of maintaining continuous abdominal bracing.\", \"Using an exaggerated hip thrust or knee bend to assist the pull-back rather than driving the return through abdominal and lat contraction.\", \"Shrugging the shoulders or losing scapular control as the arms reach the overhead position.\", \"Rolling out beyond the point at which the lumbar spine can be kept neutral, resulting in a momentary loss of spinal control at end-range.\", \"Bouncing at the bottom of the roll-out to generate rebound rather than actively reversing the movement.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Ab wheel fitted with plates loaded onto the axle sleeves and secured with collars to prevent shifting or sliding during the roll-out; performed on a non-slip surface with sufficient clear floor space in front of the lifter to accommodate full extension.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"The usable range extends from full standing to the furthest point of forward roll-out at which the lifter can still maintain a neutral, non-sagging lumbar spine; the exercise-defined limit is this point of spinal control rather than any hip or shoulder joint end-range.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"The wheel cannot be reversed back to standing while preserving a neutral spine; completing the repetition would require dropping to the knees, substituting hip flexor-driven leg movement, or hyperextending the lumbar spine to regain an upright position.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"The roll-out distance shortens noticeably, minor but still controlled trunk sag becomes visible near end-range, and the pull-back slows and requires slightly more hip involvement while spinal control is still maintained.\", \"individualization\": \"The depth of the roll-out will vary with torso length, limb proportions, shoulder mobility, and trunk strength; the appropriate depth for a given lifter is the furthest point at which the spine can still be held neutral before it begins to sag, not a fixed distance. The amount of added plate resistance may be adjusted based on individual capacity to maintain the technical standard described above. Minor adjustments in stance width for balance are acceptable provided they do not alter the sagittal-plane mechanics of the hip hinge and roll-out path.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane hip hinge and shoulder flexion/extension as the body extends forward and returns; the obliques and lateral trunk musculature act largely in an anti-lateral-flexion and anti-rotation stabilizing role in the frontal and transverse planes to control the loaded axle.\", \"starting_position\": \"Standing upright, feet hip-width apart, wheel resting on the floor directly beneath the shoulders, knees slightly softened, hands gripping the handles with arms extended toward the floor, hips hinged slightly forward, spine neutral, scapulae set without shrugging, and the abdomen braced before any movement begins.\", \"technical_failure\": \"Technical failure occurs when the lumbar spine loses its neutral position and sags into extension during the roll-out, or when the lifter can no longer generate sufficient anterior core tension to reverse the wheel back to standing without dropping to the knees, exaggerating hip drive, or hyperextending the low back to complete the return.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Glenohumeral flexion as the arms travel from beside the body to an overhead extended position during the roll-out, reversing to shoulder extension during the pull-back; scapulae protract and upwardly rotate as the arms extend overhead and retract during the return; the thoracolumbar spine resists extension (anti-extension core function) throughout; the hips move from a hinged, flexed position at end-range back to hip extension as the body returns to standing; knees remain near-extended with only slight flexion permitted for balance.\"}" |115|Low-to-High Cable Woodchopper            |"{\"grip\": \"Both hands stacked on a single handle, upper hand overlapping the lower; wrists kept neutral, not used to generate additional rotation.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Initiate the movement by rotating the pelvis and ribcage together before the arms travel.\", \"setup\": \"Stand in an athletic stance perpendicular to a low cable pulley, arms extended and hands stacked in front of the hip closest to the machine.\", \"execution\": \"Rotate the trunk and hips to drive the handle diagonally upward and across the body to above the opposite shoulder, arms following the torso rather than pulling independently.\", \"stop_when\": \"The torso can no longer generate the diagonal rotation and the arms begin to complete the range of motion alone.\"}, \"stance\": \"Athletic standing stance, feet roughly shoulder-width, weight distributed evenly to allow the back foot to pivot on its ball as the torso rotates.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain a neutral, braced spine throughout; the abdominal wall and obliques resist uncontrolled lumbar extension or lateral flexion while the pelvis and ribcage rotate together as a unit.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standing, low-to-high cable woodchopper: a diagonal, rotational trunk exercise performed against a cable anchored near floor height, with the resultant pull finishing above shoulder height on the opposite side. |104|Kneeling Ab Wheel Rollout                |"{\"grip\": \"Pronated grip on both handles, hands roughly shoulder-width apart, wrists kept relatively neutral as the wheel rolls.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the ribcage pulled down toward the pelvis so the lower back does not sag as the wheel moves away from the knees.\", \"setup\": \"Kneel on a padded surface with the ab wheel held under the shoulders, arms extended and only knees and wheel in contact with the floor.\", \"execution\": \"Roll the wheel forward by extending the shoulders and hips together while resisting lumbar extension, then pull back to the start by flexing the shoulders and hips as a unit.\", \"stop_when\": \"The lumbar spine begins to sag into extension (hips drop and low back arches) before or at the end range, or the lifter can no longer reverse the wheel back to the knees under control.\"}, \"stance\": \"Kneeling stance with knees together or hip-width apart on a padded surface; the feet may rest flat, dorsiflexed, or with toes tucked depending on individual comfort, without altering the movement pattern.\", \"bracing\": \"Brace the abdominal wall and posterior pelvic tilt slightly before initiating the roll so the pelvis and ribcage move as one unit; maintain this brace throughout to prevent the lumbar spine from extending as the lever arm lengthens.\", \"overview\": \"This is the kneeling variant of the ab wheel rollout, performed with bodyweight resistance and no additional external load. The lifter starts kneeling with hips extended over the knees and rolls the wheel forward along the floor, extending at the shoulders and hips while the trunk resists extension, then returns to the start position. Compared to standing or feet-elevated rollout variants, the kneeling version fixes the lower body against the floor, shortens the effective lever arm, and shifts a larger share of the eccentric demand onto trunk anti-extension control rather than hip flexor-driven return.\", \"eccentric\": \"Reverse the motion by pulling the wheel back toward the knees through shoulder extension combined with hip flexion, keeping the abdominal brace intact so the trunk returns as a rigid unit rather than the hips leading the pelvis into extension first.\", \"concentric\": \"From the kneeling start, allow the wheel to roll forward by flexing at the shoulders while the hips extend slightly as the body translates forward over the knees; the trunk stays rigid and moves as a single unit with the pelvis, resisting any independent lumbar extension as the lever arm increases.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Control both directions without allowing momentum to carry the wheel further than the trunk can control; a brief pause near the furthest point is acceptable but not required, and bouncing off the floor at the bottom should be avoided.\", \"end_position\": \"The rollout ends at the point where the trunk can no longer resist lumbar extension without the hips sagging toward the floor; this point varies by lifter and is not a fixed range value.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Use adequate knee padding to avoid excessive pressure on the patellar and pretibial region during kneeling.\", \"Limit forward travel to the range where lumbar extension can be actively resisted to avoid uncontrolled loading of the lower back.\", \"Ensure the ab wheel's bearing and grips are secure before loading it with body weight.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Push the wheel forward along a straight line away from the knees; pull the wheel straight back toward the knees along the same path.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Pull the ribs down toward the pelvis before and during the roll; think of the hips and ribcage moving as one block rather than the hips dropping first.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the hips to sag and the lower back to arch as the wheel reaches its furthest point.\", \"Leading the return with the hips while the shoulders lag behind, creating a whipping motion through the lumbar spine.\", \"Rolling out further than the trunk can control and using a bounce off the floor to reverse direction.\", \"Letting the elbows bend during the rollout, turning the movement into a partial press rather than a controlled trunk-driven rollout.\", \"Rushing the concentric return, causing the pelvis to extend ahead of the ribcage.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Use an ab wheel with two handles on a single axle; perform on a surface with adequate rolling traction and knee padding (mat or folded pad) to protect the knees.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"Usable range extends from the upright kneeling start to the furthest forward position at which the lifter can still initiate the return without lumbar extension collapse; the exercise-defined ROM is therefore individually limited by trunk control rather than by equipment or shoulder mobility.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to complete another repetition through the full intended ROM while keeping the pelvis and ribcage moving as a single rigid unit, distinct from being physically unable to move the wheel at all.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"The forward roll slows noticeably near the furthest controlled point, the lifter needs a longer pause before initiating the return, and slight but still controllable lumbar tension appears near the end range; full ROM and trunk rigidity are still preserved.\", \"individualization\": \"The maximum forward travel distance will vary between lifters based on trunk strength, shoulder mobility, and limb length, and should be governed by the point of lumbar control loss rather than a fixed target distance; foot and knee spacing may also be adjusted slightly for comfort without altering the core movement pattern.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane movement, combining shoulder flexion/extension with a smaller degree of hip extension/flexion as the body translates forward and backward over the knees.\", \"starting_position\": \"Kneeling upright with hips extended, knees under or slightly behind the hips, the ab wheel positioned directly beneath the shoulders, elbows extended, and the ribcage drawn down so the torso does not rest in a hyperextended lumbar position.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the pelvis tilts anteriorly and the lumbar spine extends visibly (hips sag toward the floor) as the wheel continues outward, or the lifter cannot reverse the wheel back toward the knees without this same lumbar extension occurring.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Glenohumeral flexion (rollout) and extension (return) with the arms remaining relatively fixed relative to the trunk; slight hip extension as the body moves forward and hip flexion on the return; the lumbar spine and pelvis are actively stabilized against extension throughout rather than moving through active flexion or extension.\"}" |108|Forearm Plank                            |"{\"grip\": \"Forearms rest flat on the floor in a neutral (palms-down or palms-facing-each-other) position; hands may be clasped or kept flat, whichever allows the shoulder to remain stable without discomfort.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Actively pull the ribcage down toward the pelvis and squeeze the glutes to prevent the lower back from sagging.\", \"setup\": \"Support the body on forearms and toes with elbows directly beneath the shoulders and the body forming a straight line from head to heels.\", \"execution\": \"Hold the trunk rigid and motionless by resisting extension, rotation, and lateral flexion of the spine while breathing continuously.\", \"stop_when\": \"The hips drop toward the floor or pike upward and cannot be voluntarily corrected back to a straight-line position.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet positioned hip-width to fully together, toes dorsiflexed and pressed into the floor to support the lower body; foot width does not change the target musculature meaningfully.\", \"bracing\": \"Draw the ribcage down toward the pelvis to flatten lumbar lordosis, maintain a posterior-leaning pelvic position without tucking excessively, contract the glutes to keep the hips extended, and press the forearms into the floor to keep the scapulae protracted rather than allowing them to collapse toward the spine.\", \"overview\": \"The forearm plank is a static, closed-chain anti-extension and anti-rotation exercise performed in a prone bridge position supported on the forearms and toes. This variant uses forearm (rather than hand/palm) support, which lowers the shoulder relative to the elbow and shifts more demand onto scapular stabilizers and the anterior core versus a high (straight-arm) plank. No hip or shoulder flexion/extension occurs during the hold; the task is isometric resistance to gravity-induced spinal extension and pelvic tilt.\", \"eccentric\": \"There is no eccentric phase under normal execution; deterioration of the hold (hips sagging or piking) represents a technical failure event rather than an intended movement phase.\", \"concentric\": \"There is no concentric phase; the exercise is an isometric hold. The only 'action' is the continuous, low-level muscular effort required to prevent the trunk and pelvis from deviating from the established neutral line.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Not applicable; continuous, steady breathing should be maintained throughout the hold without breath-holding or Valsalva-driven trunk shifting.\", \"end_position\": \"Identical to the starting position: a straight line from head to heel, maintained without visible sagging at the hips or excessive elevation of the pelvis.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Discontinue the hold if lumbar discomfort increases rather than attempting to push through a collapsing position.\", \"Keep the cervical spine in line with the thoracic spine rather than looking upward or tucking the chin excessively.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Keep an imaginary straight line from ear to heel; avoid letting the hips 'sink' toward or 'pike' away from the floor.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Pull the ribs down toward the hips; squeeze the glutes to keep the hips level; push the floor away through the forearms to keep the upper back broad.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the hips to sag, producing lumbar hyperextension.\", \"Piking the hips upward to unload the abdominal wall.\", \"Elbows positioned too far forward or behind the shoulder line, altering shoulder stability.\", \"Holding the breath rather than breathing continuously through the hold.\", \"Letting the head drop or crane upward, altering cervical alignment and overall trunk line.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Performed on a flat, non-slip surface; a mat may be used for elbow comfort but should not be thick enough to alter forearm-to-floor contact angle.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"None in the traditional sense; the exercise is defined by the absence of movement at the spine, pelvis, and hips throughout the hold.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"The straight-line body position can no longer be maintained or restored despite conscious effort, resulting in sustained hip sag or pike; this is distinct from simple discomfort that does not yet compromise trunk position.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Increasing visible trembling of the trunk, intermittent minor hip sagging that is still voluntarily correctable, and noticeably increased perceived effort to maintain the neutral spine position.\", \"individualization\": \"Elbow width may vary slightly (shoulder-width to slightly narrower) based on shoulder comfort, provided the elbow remains under or near the shoulder. Foot stance width may vary from together to hip-width without changing the target musculature. Hand position (clasped versus flat) is a matter of comfort and does not affect trunk mechanics.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily an isometric anti-movement task resisting sagittal-plane spinal extension and pelvic anterior tilt, with secondary isometric resistance to frontal-plane lateral flexion and transverse-plane rotation.\", \"starting_position\": \"Forearms and elbows on the floor, elbows aligned vertically beneath the shoulders, forearms parallel to each other (or hands clasped/pressed together), toes tucked under, legs extended, and the body forming a straight line from ears through shoulders, hips, and heels before the hold begins.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The pelvis drops into anterior tilt with visible lumbar extension (hip sag), or the hips rise into a piked position to reduce core demand, and the lifter is unable to voluntarily restore the straight-line position.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"No net joint motion is intended. The lumbar spine and pelvis are held in a neutral position via isometric contraction of the abdominal wall and erector spinae; the scapulae are stabilized in a mildly protracted position by serratus anterior; the shoulders are held in isometric flexion/stability with elbows fixed at roughly 90 degrees; the hips are held in near-full extension via gluteal isometric activity.\"}"
