|106|Standing Ab Wheel Rollout                |"{\"grip\": \"Pronated grip on both handles, hands approximately shoulder-width apart, wrists kept relatively neutral rather than flexed or extended under load.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Brace the abdominals hard enough to prevent the lumbar spine from arching as the hips approach the floor.\", \"setup\": \"Stand with feet hip-width apart, wheel on the floor in front of you, hands gripping the handles with arms extended and torso hip-hinged forward.\", \"execution\": \"Roll the wheel forward in a straight line as the hips and torso extend toward a near-horizontal plank, then pull the wheel back toward the feet and rise back to standing.\", \"stop_when\": \"You can no longer reverse the wheel back toward the feet without the hips sagging into lumbar hyperextension or dropping to the knees.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet hip-width apart, knees soft and allowed to flex slightly as the hips travel, feet remaining planted throughout the roll-out and return.\", \"bracing\": \"Abdominal wall braced before initiating the roll-out, ribcage drawn down toward the pelvis to prevent anterior rib flare, and a posterior pelvic tilt maintained as the hips approach the floor to prevent uncontrolled lumbar extension.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standing variant of the ab wheel rollout, performed entirely from a bent-over standing position rather than kneeling. The lifter initiates the movement from hip flexion, rolls the wheel forward until the body approaches a long, near-horizontal line from hands to feet, then pulls back to standing using trunk and lat-driven flexion rather than knee contact for support. Compared to the kneeling rollout, the lever arm is substantially longer and the hips must actively control the pike-to-extension transition, placing much greater demand on the abdominal wall, lats, and shoulder-flexor musculature to resist spinal extension throughout a larger range of motion.\", \"eccentric\": \"From the standing hip-hinge start, the wheel is rolled forward in a straight line as the hips extend and the torso lowers and lengthens, the arms traveling overhead while the abdominal wall and lats lengthen under tension to resist lumbar hyperextension and control the descent toward the low, extended position.\", \"concentric\": \"From the extended bottom position, the wheel is pulled back toward the feet as the hips flex and the torso lifts, driven by the abdominal wall and lats shortening to bring the arms and trunk back over the base of support, finishing with a return to standing.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"The roll-out and return should both be continuously controlled with no bounce or jerking reversal at the bottom position; tension on the abdominal wall and lats should remain uninterrupted throughout the range.\", \"end_position\": \"Full return to an upright standing position with the wheel drawn back near the feet and the torso vertical.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Ensure adequate clear floor space beyond the point of maximal extension to avoid collision with obstacles.\", \"Stop the repetition and reduce the roll-out depth if lower back pain or an inability to maintain a neutral spine occurs.\", \"Keep the wheel path straight to avoid lateral loss of control at the extended position.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Push the wheel out in a straight line directly away from the feet, then pull it back along the same line while pressing the feet into the floor to help rise to standing.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Brace the abdominal wall before the wheel moves, keep the ribs pulled down toward the pelvis throughout, and initiate the return by pulling the wheel back with the lats and abs rather than extending the lower back.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the hips to sag into lumbar hyperextension as the body approaches the extended bottom position.\", \"Rounding through the upper back instead of maintaining a neutral spine throughout the roll-out.\", \"Letting the wheel drift diagonally instead of tracking in a straight line away from and back toward the feet.\", \"Using a rapid bounce or jerk at the bottom of the roll-out to initiate the return instead of an active pull.\", \"Stopping the return short of full standing rather than completing hip extension at the top.\", \"Shrugging the shoulders upward instead of allowing the scapulae to protract and rotate upward under control.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"A two-handled ab wheel on a flat, non-slip floor with clear space extending roughly one and a half to two lifter-heights in front of the starting position.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"From an upright, hip-hinged start to a low point at which the torso, hips, and arms approach a single near-horizontal line with the hips close to the floor; the usable depth is defined by the point at which a neutral spine and controlled reversal can still be maintained, not by absolute proximity to the floor.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to pull the wheel back toward the feet and return to standing within the defined technical constraints, requiring the hips to drop into lumbar hyperextension, the knees to contact the floor, or a jerking motion to reverse direction.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"The roll-out distance shortens noticeably compared to earlier repetitions, a longer pause is needed at the bottom before reversing direction, and slight lumbar sag appears but can still be corrected before pulling back.\", \"individualization\": \"The depth of the roll-out and the degree of hip flexion at the start will vary with trunk length, shoulder mobility, and abdominal-lat capacity; lifters with less trunk control may stop well short of a full horizontal extension, provided the wheel path remains straight and the spine stays neutral throughout. Foot stance width may be adjusted slightly for balance without altering the intended movement pattern.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane trunk and hip flexion-extension, combined with sagittal-plane shoulder flexion of the arms as they travel from a low forward position toward overhead.\", \"starting_position\": \"Stand upright, then bend at the hips and knees to grasp the wheel handles with the wheel positioned on the floor roughly under the shoulders; torso is hip-hinged forward with a neutral spine, arms extended and elbows straight.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the lumbar spine hyperextends and the hips sag toward the floor during the roll-out, the wheel drifts off a straight forward path, or the wheel cannot be reversed back toward the feet without bouncing, using momentum, or touching a knee to the floor.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Shoulder flexion as the arms move from in front of the hips toward an overhead position; scapular upward rotation and protraction stabilized by the serratus anterior; sustained isometric elbow extension via the triceps long head; hip flexion-extension controlling the transition between the hinged start and the extended bottom position; continuous anti-extension bracing of the lumbar spine by the abdominal wall and lats rather than active spinal flexion or extension.\"}" |117|Single-Arm Dumbbell Side Bend            |"{\"grip\": \"Neutral grip on the dumbbell handle, wrist held straight in line with the forearm; grip firmness only sufficient to control the implement without inducing unwanted forearm or shoulder tension.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Move only through side-bending of the spine; keep the pelvis level and avoid rotating or leaning forward/backward.\", \"setup\": \"Stand tall holding a single dumbbell in one hand at your side, feet roughly hip-to-shoulder width apart.\", \"execution\": \"Laterally flex the spine to lower the dumbbell down the side of the thigh, then reverse the motion to return to upright by contracting the opposite-side obliques.\", \"stop_when\": \"You can no longer return to a fully upright torso position without recruiting hip hike, trunk rotation, or momentum.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet hip-width to shoulder-width apart, weight distributed evenly between both feet, knees soft but not actively bent to assist the movement.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain a level pelvis and neutral anterior-posterior spinal position throughout; avoid using the free hand or hip position to generate momentum; keep the ribcage from rotating relative to the pelvis.\", \"overview\": \"This is a unilaterally loaded lateral flexion exercise for the trunk, performed standing with a dumbbell held in one hand while the opposite hand hangs free or rests on the hip. The load creates an asymmetrical lateral flexion moment that the working-side obliques and erector spinae must control eccentrically and reverse concentrically. This variant is distinct from bilateral loaded carries or torso-rotation exercises in that the movement is confined to the frontal plane with no intended trunk rotation.\", \"eccentric\": \"Lower the torso by allowing lateral flexion toward the loaded side in a controlled manner, permitting the dumbbell to travel down the outside of the thigh while the pelvis stays level and the trunk does not rotate forward or backward.\", \"concentric\": \"From the bottom position, laterally flex the spine on the non-loaded side to raise the torso back to vertical, drawing the ribcage on the loaded side up and away from the pelvis; the dumbbell rises passively as a result of trunk motion, not from arm or shoulder action.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Perform with continuous, controlled motion in both directions; avoid using bouncing or a fast eccentric drop to generate rebound momentum for the concentric phase.\", \"end_position\": \"Torso returns to a fully vertical, neutral position with the spine straight in the frontal plane, mirroring the starting position.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Avoid excessive lateral flexion range that produces sharp or pinching discomfort in the lumbar spine.\", \"Ensure the dumbbell has a clear path along the outside of the leg to avoid contact with the knee or hip.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Slide the dumbbell straight down the outside of the thigh and pull it straight back up along the same path.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Reach the loaded-side hip toward the loaded-side shoulder to initiate the lift; keep the pelvis level as if balancing a tray on the hips.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the torso to rotate toward or away from the loaded side instead of moving strictly in the frontal plane.\", \"Hiking the hip on the loaded side to substitute for spinal lateral flexion.\", \"Leaning forward or backward at the trunk during the descent or ascent.\", \"Using the free hand to push off the thigh to assist the return to upright.\", \"Limiting range of motion to a small partial bend that does not meaningfully load the obliques.\", \"Bouncing at the bottom position to use momentum rather than controlled muscular reversal.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"A single dumbbell of appropriate size to allow full unobstructed motion along the outside of the thigh without contacting the floor or requiring knee flexion to clear it.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"Bounded by the individual's comfortable lateral spinal flexion, typically from an upright neutral position down to the point where the dumbbell reaches the mid-to-lower thigh; depth should stop short of any point requiring trunk rotation or hip shift to continue the descent.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to return the torso to a vertical, non-rotated position using lateral flexion alone within the established range of motion, even though the dumbbell could still be moved through compensatory patterns.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Noticeably slower ascent back to vertical, slight increase in effort to keep the pelvis level, but full range of motion and frontal-plane path still preserved.\", \"individualization\": \"The comfortable depth of lateral flexion varies with individual spinal mobility and trunk length; deeper bends are acceptable provided the pelvis stays level and no rotation occurs. Hand position of the non-loaded arm (resting on hip versus hanging free) may vary based on comfort without altering the exercise. Stance width may be adjusted slightly for balance, particularly with heavier dumbbells.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily frontal-plane lateral flexion of the lumbar and lower thoracic spine, with the hips and lower extremities remaining largely fixed.\", \"starting_position\": \"Stand upright with feet approximately hip-width apart, one dumbbell held in one hand with the arm hanging naturally at the side, palm facing the thigh. The opposite hand may rest lightly on the hip or hang free. Spine is vertical, pelvis level, shoulders stacked over hips.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the torso can no longer be returned to upright through lateral spinal flexion alone, requiring trunk rotation, hip shift, forward/backward lean, or use of the free hand pushing off the leg to complete the motion.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Lateral flexion and extension of the spine (intervertebral segments, predominantly lumbar) toward and away from the loaded side; the hip and knee joints act as stabilizers rather than movers; the shoulder and elbow of the loaded arm remain relatively fixed, transmitting the dumbbell's weight rather than actively producing motion.\"}" |105|Weighted Kneeling Ab Wheel Rollout       |"{\"grip\": \"Pronated grip on both handles, hands roughly shoulder-width apart, wrists kept straight rather than extended under load.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Resist lumbar hyperextension and hip sag as the wheel moves away from the body.\", \"setup\": \"Kneel on a padded surface with a plate loaded and secured on the ab wheel's central axle, hands gripping the handles directly beneath the shoulders.\", \"execution\": \"Roll the wheel forward under control until the trunk approaches the floor while maintaining a braced, neutral spine, then pull the wheel back toward the knees to return to the upright kneeling position.\", \"stop_when\": \"The hips begin to sag toward the floor or the lifter cannot reverse direction from the forward position without the lumbar spine losing its neutral, braced posture.\"}, \"stance\": \"Kneeling with knees hip-width apart; toes may be pointed or flexed depending on floor surface and comfort.\", \"bracing\": \"Brace the abdominal wall as if anticipating an impact, maintain a posterior pelvic tilt bias to prevent lumbar sag, and actively contract the glutes to hold the hips extended and in line with the torso throughout the movement.\", \"overview\": \"This is a kneeling ab wheel rollout performed with additional resistance created by a weight plate loaded and secured onto the wheel's central axle sleeve, rather than by adding load to the torso. The added rotational mass increases the effort required both to control the forward roll and to pull the wheel back, without changing the fundamental kneeling rollout pattern. This distinguishes it from bodyweight kneeling rollouts and from standing or barbell rollout variants, which alter lever length and hip mechanics substantially.\", \"eccentric\": \"Allow the wheel to roll forward by permitting controlled glenohumeral flexion while the abdominal wall resists the extension moment created by the moving load; the torso lowers toward the floor as the hips remain extended and the lumbar spine stays neutral rather than arching.\", \"concentric\": \"From the extended position, pull the wheel back toward the knees by extending the shoulders and contracting the lats and abdominals together, keeping the hips extended and the spine in the same braced position established at setup; the torso rises back toward vertical without the hips leading the movement.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Maintain continuous control throughout the forward roll rather than letting the added plate mass accelerate the wheel; a brief pause at the furthest controllable point is acceptable before initiating the pull-back.\", \"end_position\": \"Kneeling upright with the wheel back near the knees, hips stacked over the knees, and the torso vertical.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Confirm the plate is locked in place on the wheel's axle with a collar before each set to prevent lateral shifting during the roll.\", \"Limit forward ROM to the point where lumbar neutrality and hip extension can still be maintained to avoid uncontrolled collapse toward the floor.\", \"Use adequate knee padding given the sustained kneeling contact point under load.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Push the wheel forward without letting the hips drop toward the floor; pull the wheel back toward the knees along the same path it rolled out on.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Brace the abdomen before initiating the roll; keep pulling the ribs down toward the pelvis rather than letting the low back arch; drive the pull-back through the lats and abs simultaneously.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the hips to sag toward the floor as the wheel reaches its furthest point, producing lumbar hyperextension.\", \"Rolling out beyond the range at which the abdominal wall can maintain a braced, neutral spine.\", \"Leading the return phase with hip flexion rather than shoulder extension and lat/ab contraction.\", \"Bouncing off the bottom position instead of controlling the transition from forward roll to pull-back.\", \"Using a hand width narrow enough to place the wrists into excessive extension under load.\", \"Failing to secure the loaded plate on the wheel's axle, causing it to shift during the roll.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Use an ab wheel with a loadable center sleeve; load a weight plate onto the axle and lock it with the retaining collar so it cannot shift laterally during the roll. Place a mat or pad under the knees.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"The usable range extends from the upright kneeling start to the point of maximal forward reach at which the lumbar spine and pelvis can still be held stable without sagging; this endpoint is determined by the lifter's core control rather than by the equipment.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to pull the wheel back to the upright kneeling position while maintaining hip extension and a neutral lumbar spine, regardless of whether some alternative body motion could still move the wheel.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"The return phase becomes noticeably slower and more effortful, the forward reach shortens slightly, and minor but still recoverable loss of lumbar bracing may appear at the deepest point without full hip sag.\", \"individualization\": \"Hand width may vary slightly with shoulder width provided the wrists remain straight and the wheel tracks in a straight sagittal line. The maximal forward reach distance will vary with torso length, shoulder flexion mobility, and abdominal strength, and should be set individually at the point where lumbar bracing can still be preserved rather than at a fixed distance. The amount of plate loading is a resistance parameter and does not change the technical execution described here.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane movement combining glenohumeral flexion/extension with anti-extension trunk control; a smaller frontal-plane stabilization component is present at the hips and shoulders to prevent lateral drift of the wheel.\", \"starting_position\": \"Kneel with the hips stacked over the knees, knees roughly hip-width apart, wheel positioned on the floor directly beneath the shoulders, arms extended, torso vertical, and pelvis in a neutral, slightly posteriorly tilted position.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the hips sag toward the floor, the lumbar spine moves into visible hyperextension, or the lifter cannot reverse the wheel's direction from the forward position without collapsing the torso toward the ground.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Glenohumeral flexion during the forward roll and extension during the return; elbow extension held isometrically throughout; scapular protraction and upward rotation via serratus anterior as the arms reach overhead; the lumbar spine and pelvis are held in a fixed, anti-extension position by the abdominal wall and glutes rather than moving through active flexion or extension.\"}" |113|Hanging Bent-Knee Pelvic Raise           |"{\"grip\": \"Pronated grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder width; grip width is not a primary technical variable in this exercise.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Finish each repetition with a deliberate posterior pelvic tilt, not just hip flexion.\", \"setup\": \"Hang from a fixed bar with a pronated grip and shoulders actively depressed rather than passively stretched.\", \"execution\": \"Flex the hips to bring the bent knees toward the chest, then continue by posteriorly tilting the pelvis to curl the tailbone upward before reversing under control.\", \"stop_when\": \"You can no longer produce a visible pelvic curl at the top and the movement becomes a swing-assisted knee raise.\"}, \"stance\": \"Knees bent throughout, ankles kept together or close together, hips and knees moving as a unit.\", \"bracing\": \"Scapulae depressed and lightly retracted before initiating movement to prevent shoulder impingement and body swing; anterior abdominal wall pre-tensed to control the transition from hip flexion into pelvic tilt.\", \"overview\": \"This variant is a hanging bent-knee raise in which the terminal portion of the repetition is driven by posterior pelvic tilt (lumbar flexion) rather than by hip flexion alone, increasing the contribution of the rectus abdominis beyond that of a standard hanging knee raise. |127|Machine Hip Thrust                       |"{\"grip\": \"Hands typically hold the side handles or seat edges only to stabilize the torso against the pad; grip does not contribute to force production.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Push the pelvis toward the ceiling by contracting the glutes rather than arching the lower back to move the pad.\", \"setup\": \"Sit into the machine with the upper back/shoulder blades braced against the support pad and the hip pad positioned low across the pelvis, feet flat on the platform at roughly hip width.\", \"execution\": \"Drive the hips upward into extension against the pad while the torso stays fixed against the backrest, then lower under control back to the start.\", \"stop_when\": \"The hips can no longer reach full extension without the lumbar spine hyperextending to complete the range.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet flat, approximately hip- to shoulder-width apart, toes pointed slightly outward or straight ahead depending on hip structure.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain contact between the upper back and the pad throughout the set, keep the ribcage aligned over the pelvis, and avoid using lumbar extension to substitute for hip extension as the pad rises.\", \"overview\": \"This is a back-supported selectorized machine hip thrust in which the lifter is seated with the torso stabilized against a fixed pad and drives a hip-level pad upward through hip extension. |46 |Dumbbell Wrist Extension                 |"{\"grip\": \"Use a closed pronated grip around the dumbbells with enough finger tension to prevent slipping. The defining movement is isolated wrist extension against gravity while the elbows, forearms, and upper arms remain essentially stationary. Unlike a forearm curl with active elbow movement, the dumbbells move primarily because the hands rotate at the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints.\", \"eccentric\": \"Lower the dumbbells under control by allowing the wrists to flex while the forearms remain fixed on the support. Observable breakdowns include lifting the forearms from the support, moving the elbows or shoulders, using trunk momentum, excessive radial or ulnar deviation, dropping the dumbbells through the eccentric, or substantially shortening the wrist excursion.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"During the concentric phase, the wrists extend while the forearms remain pronated and the elbows remain essentially fixed. |135|Dumbbell Reverse Lunge                   |"{\"grip\": \"Neutral (palms facing the body), grip firm enough to control the dumbbells without excessive forearm tension.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Load the front leg by keeping the front shin close to vertical and the torso upright throughout the descent.\", \"setup\": \"Stand upright holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, feet hip-width apart.\", \"execution\": \"Step one leg backward into a lunge until the rear knee approaches the floor, then drive back up through the front leg to standing, alternating legs each repetition.\", \"stop_when\": \"You can no longer control the descent of the rear knee toward the floor or the front knee drifts sharply inward on the drive up.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet begin hip-width apart; during the lunge the working (front) leg remains under the hip while the trailing leg steps directly backward along a similar hip-width line rather than crossing the midline.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain a neutral spine with the ribcage aligned over the pelvis throughout the step-back and return; avoid trunk lean forward or lateral tilt as the rear knee lowers.\", \"overview\": \"This is a bilateral alternating reverse lunge performed with dumbbells held at the sides in a neutral grip, alternating the working leg between repetitions. |133|Belt Squat                               |"{\"grip\": \"Hands rest on the machine's handles or frame purely for balance; no pulling or pushing force should be transmitted through the arms during the repetition.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the torso upright and ribcage stacked over the pelvis so the resistance vector stays through the hips rather than the spine.\", \"setup\": \"Stand on the raised platform with the belt pad positioned over the hips/iliac crests and the loading carriage hanging below, holding the frame handles only for balance.\", \"execution\": \"Squat by flexing the hips and knees to lower the belt-loaded carriage, then drive through the feet to extend hips and knees back to standing.\", \"stop_when\": \"The heels lift, the torso pitches sharply forward, or full squat depth can no longer be reached without those compensations.\"}, \"stance\": \"Shoulder-width to moderately wider stance with feet turned outward roughly 10-20 degrees; exact width may vary with hip structure provided knee tracking follows the line of the toes.\", \"bracing\": \"Brace the abdominal wall and keep the ribcage aligned over the pelvis before initiating the descent; maintain this alignment throughout to prevent the torso from folding forward as the carriage load increases.\", \"overview\": \"This is the plate-loaded belt squat performed on a dedicated belt squat machine, where resistance is applied through a hip belt connected to a plate-loaded lever or carriage beneath a raised standing platform rather than through the spine or shoulders. Because the load path runs through the belt at hip level, the torso can remain more upright than in a barbell back squat and the hands are used only for balance on the frame handles, not for force transmission. This variant emphasizes knee- and hip-extensor work with minimal axial spinal loading compared to barbell or hack squat variants.\", \"eccentric\": \"Flex the hips and knees to lower the carriage under control, allowing the torso to remain upright with only a slight, consistent forward lean; the descent path should mirror the ascent path rather than shifting the knees or hips laterally.\", \"concentric\": \"Drive through the full foot to extend the hips and knees simultaneously, raising the belt-loaded carriage and returning to standing. The torso should rise with the hips rather than the hips shooting upward while the torso remains folded forward.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Maintain continuous, controlled tension through the belt attachment; avoid bouncing the carriage at the bottom of the range to reverse direction.\", \"end_position\": \"Standing tall with hips and knees fully extended, carriage at the top of its travel, and torso upright without lumbar hyperextension.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Ensure the belt pad is centered over the hips and not riding onto soft tissue or the lower abdomen before beginning the set.\", \"Confirm the carriage and platform are securely engaged and level before loading additional plates.\", \"Avoid using the handles to yank the torso upright, which can mask a loss of hip/knee extension control.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Push the platform away from you as you rise; keep the belt attachment point directly beneath the hips throughout the movement.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Sit the hips down and back between the knees while keeping the chest tall; drive the feet into the platform to stand up.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the torso to fold forward as the load increases instead of keeping the ribcage stacked over the pelvis.\", \"Pulling on the frame handles to assist the ascent rather than using them only for balance.\", \"Letting the heels rise off the platform near the bottom of the range.\", \"Knees caving inward during the ascent.\", \"Terminating the descent before reaching the intended depth as fatigue increases.\", \"Bouncing the carriage at the bottom to generate momentum for the ascent.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Adjust the belt strap length so the pad sits snugly at the level of the iliac crests/greater trochanters when standing on the platform, with the carriage or lever arm loaded with the intended plates. Confirm the platform height allows sufficient clearance for the carriage to travel through the full intended range without bottoming out prematurely.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"From full standing extension down to the depth at which the thighs are approximately parallel to the platform or as limited by carriage travel, provided the heels remain in contact with the platform and the torso maintains its upright alignment throughout.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to complete another repetition to the working depth and back to full hip/knee extension without the heels rising, the torso collapsing forward, or the knees deviating from their tracking line.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Noticeably slower ascent, increased reliance on the handles for balance, and a slight but recoverable increase in forward lean while full depth and heel contact are still maintained.\", \"individualization\": \"Stance width and foot angle may vary with hip and ankle structure provided the knees track in line with the toes throughout the range. Squat depth may be adjusted within the carriage's travel based on individual hip and ankle mobility, and belt height may require minor adjustment for torso length, provided the resistance vector remains centered over the hips rather than shifting toward the lumbar spine.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane hip and knee flexion-extension, with ankle dorsiflexion/plantarflexion accompanying the descent and ascent; minimal frontal- or transverse-plane motion at the trunk.\", \"starting_position\": \"Stand on the platform with feet placed to allow unobstructed downward travel of the belt attachment, hips directly under the belt pad, torso upright, knees slightly unlocked, and hands resting lightly on the frame handles.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the heels lift off the platform, the torso pitches forward substantially beyond its starting alignment, the knees collapse inward, or the lifter can no longer reach the working depth while maintaining an upright, balanced torso position.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Hip flexion during the descent and hip extension during the ascent; knee flexion during the descent and knee extension during the ascent; ankle dorsiflexion during the descent with plantarflexion assistance near lockout. The lumbar spine is held in a relatively fixed neutral position throughout, and the upper extremities act isometrically to stabilize balance via the frame handles rather than to move the load.\"}" |123|Dumbbell Romanian Deadlift               |"{\"grip\": \"Pronated grip on both dumbbells, arms fully extended and relaxed at the shoulder so the load hangs directly below the shoulders throughout the movement.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Push the hips backward as far as possible before the torso is allowed to lower.\", \"setup\": \"Stand holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of the thighs, feet hip-width apart, knees softly flexed and fixed for the set.\", \"execution\": \"Hinge at the hips to lower the dumbbells along the front of the thighs while the spine stays neutral, then drive the hips forward to return to standing.\", \"stop_when\": \"The lumbar spine begins to round or the hips can no longer travel rearward without the knees bending further.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet roughly hip-width apart, toes forward or very slightly turned out; stance width may vary but should allow the dumbbells to pass close to the body without hitting the knees.\", \"bracing\": \"Brace the abdominal wall and maintain a neutral lumbar curve before initiating the hinge; keep the ribcage aligned over the pelvis and avoid allowing the lower back to round or hyperextend as the hips move backward.\", \"overview\": \"This is a bilateral dumbbell Romanian deadlift, a hip-hinge exercise performed from a standing position with the dumbbells held at arm's length rather than pulled from the floor. Knee flexion is minimal and fixed throughout the repetition, distinguishing it from a conventional or stiff-leg deadlift variant that begins from the floor. The exercise trains the hip extensors and posterior chain through a hip-dominant range of motion limited by hamstring length and the ability to keep the spine neutral, with the dumbbells traveling close to the body along the thighs and shins.\", \"eccentric\": \"Initiate by pushing the hips straight back while allowing the torso to incline forward; the dumbbells travel back up along the front of the thighs to the starting position.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Lower under continuous control without bouncing at the bottom; the reversal from eccentric to concentric should be driven by hip extension rather than momentum from the upper body.\", \"end_position\": \"Standing fully upright with hips extended, glutes contracted, and the dumbbells back against the front of the thighs.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Stop the descent as soon as the lumbar spine loses its neutral position, regardless of how far the dumbbells have traveled.\", \"Keep the dumbbells close to the legs throughout to avoid excessive spinal loading from an extended moment arm.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Keep the dumbbells brushing lightly against the thighs on the way down; no bench, block, or other equipment is required.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"Bounded by hamstring flexibility and the ability to maintain a neutral spine; the descent stops at the point where further hip flexion would require lumbar rounding, not at a fixed dumbbell height or floor contact.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to complete another repetition through the full available hip-hinge range while keeping the lumbar spine neutral and the knee angle essentially fixed, regardless of whether the dumbbells could still be moved using lumbar flexion or a knee-bending pull.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"The hinge depth becomes slightly shallower, hip drive on the concentric feels noticeably slower, and there is a mild but still controlled tendency for the lower back to want to round at the bottom.\", \"individualization\": \"Hip-hinge depth and the fixed knee angle will vary with hamstring flexibility, torso-to-leg proportions, and hip mobility; a lifter with longer femurs or tighter hamstrings will reach spinal-neutral limit at a higher dumbbell position, while others may hinge closer to mid-shin. Stance width and slight toe-out may be adjusted for comfort provided the dumbbells continue to track close to the body and the knee angle remains essentially constant throughout the repetition.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane hip flexion and extension, with the trunk and dumbbells moving as a single unit relative to the pelvis.\", \"starting_position\": \"Standing upright, feet approximately hip-width apart, knees with a small, fixed bend, dumbbells resting against the front of the thighs, shoulders retracted slightly, spine in neutral, gaze directed forward or slightly down.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the lumbar spine rounds, the hips stop translating rearward and the knees begin bending substantially to continue the descent, or the torso can no longer return to upright without lumbar hyperextension or momentum from jerking the dumbbells.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Hip flexion during the eccentric phase and hip extension during the concentric phase, with the knee held in a small, largely unchanging degree of flexion; the lumbar spine and thoracic spine act isometrically to preserve neutral alignment while the shoulders stabilize the arms holding the dumbbells.\"}" |125|Barbell Good Morning                     |"{\"grip\": \"Hands gripping the bar just outside shoulder width, pulling down slightly on the bar to keep it locked against the back rather than resting passively; wrists neutral.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Initiate and control the movement through hip flexion/extension, not lumbar or knee flexion.\", \"setup\": \"Bar rests across the rear deltoids/upper trapezius as in a low-bar squat position, feet hip-to-shoulder width, knees with a slight, fixed bend.\", \"execution\": \"Hinge at the hips to push the hips backward while the torso lowers toward parallel with the floor, then drive the hips forward to return upright.\", \"stop_when\": \"The lumbar spine begins to round or the knees start bending further to compensate for hip mobility limits.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet hip-to-shoulder width, toes pointing forward or very slightly outward, weight distributed through the middle to rear of the foot.\", \"bracing\": \"Abdominal brace maintained throughout to resist spinal flexion under load; ribcage kept stacked over the pelvis; glutes engaged at the top; the fixed knee angle is held isometrically so the hips, not the knees, produce the movement.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standard standing barbell good morning: a hip-hinge exercise performed with the bar on the upper back and a slight, fixed knee bend maintained throughout, distinguishing it from both the stiff-legged variant (near-locked knees, greater hamstring stretch emphasis) and the squat-style good morning (deeper knee bend with quads more heavily involved). ascent continues until full hip extension and an upright torso are reached.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"The lifter cannot complete another repetition through the full intended range while keeping the spine neutral and the knee angle fixed; \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane hip flexion and extension, with the trunk and bar traveling forward and downward, then backward and upward, along a path that stays close to the body.\", \"starting_position\": \"Standing with the bar resting on the upper trapezius/rear deltoid shelf (as in a low-bar back squat), feet set at hip-to-shoulder width, knees slightly bent and fixed |119|Dumbbell Suitcase Carry                  |"{\"grip\": \"Neutral (parallel) grip on the dumbbell handle with the wrist held straight; the arm hangs naturally at the side without active elbow flexion beyond what the dumbbell's length requires.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Prevent the trunk from leaning toward the dumbbell and prevent the hip on the loaded side from dropping with each step.\", \"setup\": \"Hold a single dumbbell in one hand at your side with a neutral grip, standing tall with shoulders level and pelvis neutral.\", \"execution\": \"Walk forward with a normal gait while keeping the trunk upright and the pelvis level despite the one-sided load.\", \"stop_when\": \"You can no longer keep the shoulders level and the pelvis from dropping/hiking with each stride, or grip begins to fail.\"}, \"stance\": \"Hip-width stance at rest, transitioning into a normal walking gait with feet tracking forward in a straight line rather than widened for balance.\", \"bracing\": \"Brace the obliques on the loaded side to resist trunk lateral flexion toward the dumbbell, keep the ribcage stacked over the pelvis, and actively resist hip drop on the stance leg through the gluteus medius and minimus; avoid shrugging the shoulder on the loaded side upward toward the ear.\", \"overview\": \"This is the unilateral (single-arm) variant of the suitcase carry: one dumbbell is carried at arm's length beside the body while walking, with the opposite hand empty. Unlike the double-arm suitcase carry, the asymmetric load creates a one-sided frontal-plane challenge, requiring active anti-lateral-flexion of the trunk and pelvic stabilization to prevent the hip from dropping toward the loaded side. It differs from a farmer's carry primarily in that only one implement is used, making trunk and hip control—rather than raw axial loading—the dominant technical demand.\", \"eccentric\": \"Similarly, there is no lowering phase during the carry itself; each step's weight-acceptance phase (foot strike and loading response) requires the same anti-lateral-flexion and anti-hip-drop control as the propulsive phase, so control must be maintained continuously through the gait cycle rather than only at a discrete point.\", \"concentric\": \"There is no lifting phase in the traditional sense; the loaded 'work' phase is each stride's stance and push-off, during which the trunk and pelvis must actively resist the lateral pull of the dumbbell as weight shifts over the stance leg.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Walk at a steady, controlled pace; avoid rushing steps to mask loss of trunk or pelvic control, and avoid letting the dumbbell swing forward-backward with stride momentum.\", \"end_position\": \"The carry concludes when the designated distance or duration is reached, or earlier if postural control can no longer be maintained; the dumbbell is then lowered to the ground under control or set down to switch hands, without dropping it.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Ensure the walking path is clear of obstacles and other people given the extended time carrying a loaded implement.\", \"Set the dumbbell down under control at the end of the carry rather than dropping it near the feet.\", \"Stop and reset grip if the dumbbell begins to slip rather than allowing it to swing uncontrolled.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Walk as if balancing a full glass of water on each shoulder; keep the dumbbell hanging straight down without swinging forward or back.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Resist leaning away from the dumbbell; keep the pelvis level with each step; keep the loaded shoulder pulled down away from the ear.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Leaning the trunk laterally away from the dumbbell to counterbalance the load.\", \"Allowing the hip on the loaded side to drop with each step instead of keeping the pelvis level.\", \"Hiking or shrugging the shoulder on the loaded side upward toward the ear.\", \"Letting the dumbbell swing forward and backward with stride rhythm instead of hanging still.\", \"Rotating the trunk or shoulders to compensate for the one-sided load.\", \"Widening the stance or shortening stride length to artificially stabilize the pelvis.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"A single dumbbell of appropriate size and handle length, and a clear, sufficiently long walking path free of obstacles.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"There is minimal joint range of motion at the shoulder, elbow, or wrist; the exercise-defined 'range' is the gait cycle itself, with trunk lateral flexion and pelvic drop kept to a visually negligible amount throughout each stride.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"RIR 0 is reached when the lifter can no longer maintain a level pelvis and upright trunk within the technical standard for even a few additional steps, distinct from complete inability to hold the dumbbell at all.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Increasing but still correctable trunk lean or pelvic drop, a shortening or slowing stride, and early grip fatigue (dumbbell shifting slightly in the hand) suggest the carry is nearing its technical limit, though this cannot be judged with complete precision.\", \"individualization\": \"Stride length, natural gait width, and the degree of arm swing on the unloaded side may vary between lifters based on anthropometry and gait mechanics, provided the pelvis remains level and the trunk avoids pronounced lateral flexion. A small, symmetrical degree of natural postural sway is acceptable and should not be confused with progressive loss of pelvic or trunk control.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane locomotion (walking gait) superimposed on a frontal-plane stabilization demand, as the trunk and pelvis resist lateral flexion and hip drop caused by the one-sided load.\", \"starting_position\": \"Stand upright with feet approximately hip-width apart, the dumbbell held at arm's length beside one hip, shoulders level, ribcage stacked over the pelvis, and gaze forward.\", \"technical_failure\": \"Technical failure occurs when the trunk visibly and repeatedly leans away from or toward the dumbbell, when the hip on the loaded side noticeably drops or hikes with each step, when the gait pattern breaks down (widened stance, side-stepping, trunk rotation), or when grip begins to slip and the dumbbell must be actively caught or repositioned.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"The shoulder, elbow, and wrist remain in a largely static, loaded position (shoulder near neutral adduction/extension, elbow slightly flexed, wrist in a fixed neutral grip) while the hips, knees, and ankles cycle through normal gait flexion/extension. The lumbar spine and pelvis are held isometrically near neutral, resisting lateral flexion toward the load and resisting frontal-plane hip drop on the stance leg opposite the load.\"}" |126|Barbell Hip Thrust                       |"{\"grip\": \"Both hands grip the barbell just outside the hips to stabilize the bar against rolling; grip width is not a primary technical variable.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Push the feet into the floor and drive the hips toward the ceiling rather than arching the lower back to finish the range.\", \"setup\": \"Upper back supported on the edge of a bench, barbell padded and positioned directly over the hip crease, feet flat on the floor at roughly shin-vertical shin angle.\", \"execution\": \"Drive the hips upward by extending through the hips until the torso and thighs form a straight line, then lower under control without resting the glutes on the floor between reps.\", \"stop_when\": \"The lockout position can no longer be reached without the lumbar spine hyperextending to compensate for insufficient hip extension.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet placed roughly hip- to shoulder-width apart, toes pointed forward or turned out slightly, positioned so that at the top of the movement the shins are approximately vertical.\", \"bracing\": \"Ribcage kept stacked over the pelvis with a posterior pelvic tilt maintained at the top position; abdominal wall braced to prevent the lumbar spine from hyperextending as hip extension nears completion.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standard bench-supported barbell hip thrust, in which the upper back (roughly scapula level) rests against a bench while the barbell is loaded across the hips and the feet remain planted on the floor throughout. neutral-to-slightly-posteriorly-tilted position.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The lifter can no longer reach full hip extension without substituting lumbar hyperextension, pelvic anterior tilt, or a lifting of the upper back off the bench to complete the range.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Hip extension as the primary joint action, produced mainly by the gluteus maximus and hamstrings; the |131|Hack Squat                               |"{\"grip\": \"Hands rest on the side handles or frame primarily for postural reference and minor stabilization; grip does not contribute to force production.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the entire back and hips pinned against the pads throughout the descent so only the sled travels, not the torso.\", \"setup\": \"Back and shoulders flat against the angled pads with feet placed centrally on the platform, roughly hip-width apart.\", \"execution\": \"Bend the hips and knees to lower the sled along its fixed rail, then drive through the feet to extend back to the start.\", \"stop_when\": \"The lower back or hips begin to lift off the pad, or the knees can no longer track over the toes without collapsing inward.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet placed centrally on the platform at hip-width, toes pointed slightly outward; this central placement favors quadriceps loading relative to a high or wide-foot variant.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain firm contact between the upper back, shoulders, and pelvis against the pads throughout the set; brace the abdominals to prevent the lumbar spine from rounding away from the pad as the hips flex.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standard plate-loaded linear hack squat performed on a fixed-rail sled machine, where the lifter's torso is braced against an angled back pad and the shoulders are secured under padded supports while the feet remain on a stationary platform and the loaded sled travels along a diagonal track. The fixed bar path removes the balance and trunk-stabilization demands of a free-standing squat, allowing near-exclusive focus on hip and knee flexion-extension under a predetermined trajectory. Foot placement is assumed central and moderately narrow, producing pronounced quadriceps recruitment (particularly vastus lateralis and vastus medialis) with secondary gluteal and adductor contribution; this distinguishes it from high-foot or wide-stance hack squat variants that shift emphasis posteriorly.\", \"eccentric\": \"Allow the sled to lower under control by flexing the knees and hips together, keeping the back and hips in continuous contact with the pad and the knees tracking in line with the toes as the sled descends.\", \"concentric\": \"Drive through the full foot to extend the knees and hips simultaneously, pushing the sled up along the fixed rail until the knees reach a stable, near-full extension without locking forcefully.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Avoid bouncing the sled off the lower stops; a brief pause at the bottom before reversing direction helps confirm the depth is controlled rather than momentum-driven.\", \"end_position\": \"Knees approaching full extension with hips fully extended, sled at the top of its stable travel with tension maintained through the quadriceps.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Engage the mechanical safety catches before loading or unloading plates.\", \"Do not release the safety stops until the shoulders and back are fully seated against the pads.\", \"Avoid descending past the point where the hips lift off the pad, as this shifts load onto the lumbar spine in a position the machine is not designed to support.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Drive the sled straight up the rail; keep the knees traveling over the second and third toes.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Push the platform away through the whole foot; keep the pelvis glued to the pad as the knees bend.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Allowing the hips to lift off the pad at the bottom of the descent, converting the movement into a partial good-morning pattern.\", \"Letting the knees drift inward during the concentric drive under heavier loads.\", \"Using a rapid bounce off the bottom stops instead of controlling the transition.\", \"Placing the feet too high on the platform, which shifts load posteriorly and changes the intended quad-dominant emphasis.\", \"Locking the knees aggressively at the top rather than stopping at stable extension.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Adjust the shoulder pads so they contact just above the deltoids without forcing the neck into flexion, and set the footplate distance so the knees track over the toes at the bottom of the intended range. Load plates symmetrically on both sides of the carriage.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"Descend until the hip crease approaches knee level or until the lower back begins to lift off the pad, whichever occurs first; the effective ROM is therefore individually limited by hip and ankle mobility rather than a fixed depth marker.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to extend the knees and hips through the intended depth without the hips lifting off the pad or the knees collapsing inward, even though the sled could still be moved using compensatory positioning.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Sled velocity slows noticeably during the concentric drive, the lifter requires a longer pause at the bottom to initiate the ascent, but full contact with the pads and intended depth are still preserved.\", \"individualization\": \"Foot position within the central range, stance width, and toe angle may vary moderately with hip structure and ankle mobility, provided the knees continue to track over the toes and the back remains against the pad. Depth achieved before the hips lift off the pad will vary with individual hip and ankle mobility and should not be forced beyond that point.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Sagittal-plane hip and knee flexion-extension constrained to the machine's fixed diagonal rail; no meaningful frontal- or transverse-plane movement occurs due to the guided track.\", \"starting_position\": \"Stand under the shoulder pads with the upper back and sacrum flat against the angled backrest, feet flat on the platform roughly hip-width apart, knees extended but not locked, and the sled fully supported at the top of the rail before the safety catches are released.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the lower back or hips separate from the pad, the knees deviate medially under load, or the descent depth must be shortened to complete the repetition.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Knee flexion-extension and hip flexion-extension along a fixed diagonal path; ankle dorsiflexion-plantarflexion occurs passively as the foot remains flat on the platform; the spine and shoulders act as stabilizers against the pads rather than moving segments.\"}" |130|Smith Machine Back Squat                 |"{\"grip\": \"Hands positioned just outside shoulder width on the bar, primarily to stabilize its position across the back rather than to bear load.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the torso upright and let the knees track forward over the toes so the bar path stays aligned with the machine's rail without needing anteroposterior balance corrections.\", \"setup\": \"Position the bar across the upper trapezius with feet set slightly forward of the bar's vertical track, allowing a near-vertical torso throughout the movement.\", \"execution\": \"Squat straight down by flexing the knees and hips while the bar travels on its fixed vertical rail, then drive back up through the feet to full knee and hip extension.\", \"stop_when\": \"The knees can no longer complete the descent-to-ascent path without the hips shooting back to unload the quadriceps or the heels lifting off the floor.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet approximately shoulder-width apart, toes turned out slightly, positioned forward of the bar's rail so that the torso can remain close to vertical without the heels lifting.\", \"bracing\": \"Brace the abdominal wall moderately to maintain a neutral spine, but note that trunk stabilization demand is lower than in a free-standing squat because the bar cannot drift forward or backward.\", \"overview\": \"This is a Smith machine back squat performed with a relatively forward foot placement relative to the bar's fixed vertical path, producing an upright torso and a quadriceps-dominant knee-flexion pattern rather than a hip-hinge-dominant free-barbell squat. Because the bar is constrained to a vertical rail, the lifter does not need to balance it fore-aft, which reduces erector spinae and oblique stabilization demands compared to a free-weight back squat. This variant is distinguished from a free-standing high-bar or low-bar squat primarily by the fixed bar trajectory and the resulting shift toward knee-dominant mechanics.\", \"eccentric\": \"Lower under control by flexing the knees and hips together, allowing the knees to travel forward over the toes while the torso stays upright, mirroring the ascent path in reverse.\", \"concentric\": \"Drive through the whole foot to extend the knees and hips simultaneously, pushing the bar upward along its fixed vertical path until the knees and hips reach full extension; the torso angle should remain essentially unchanged from the bottom position.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Control the descent without bouncing out of the bottom position; a brief pause at the bottom is acceptable but not required since the fixed bar path does not create momentum-related instability the way a free bar does.\", \"end_position\": \"Full knee and hip extension with the bar directly overhead of its rail contact point and the torso vertical, without hyperextending the lumbar spine.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Set the Smith machine safety hooks or pins at a height just below the intended bottom position before beginning the set.\", \"Ensure the bar is fully rotated and locked onto the rail hooks before stepping out from under it at the end of the set.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Keep the bar traveling in a straight vertical line without pressing it forward or backward against the rail; safety catches should be set just below the intended bottom position of the squat.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"Descend until the hip crease reaches approximately the level of the knee or as deep as can be achieved while keeping the heels flat and the lumbar spine neutral; depth is limited by the lifter's ankle and hip mobility rather than by the machine.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to complete the ascent to full knee and hip extension while keeping the heels down and the torso in its established upright position, distinct from simply being unable to move the bar at all.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Noticeably slower ascent velocity, a small increase in knee valgus or heel pressure shift, but the torso angle and full range of motion are still maintained.\", \"individualization\": \"Foot distance forward of the bar's vertical track may vary with tibia length, ankle dorsiflexion range, and hip structure, provided the torso remains upright and the heels stay in contact with the floor throughout the range of motion. Stance width and toe angle may also be adjusted moderately for hip comfort without altering the fundamental knee-dominant mechanics of this variant.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane triple flexion/extension of the hip, knee, and ankle, with the bar itself restricted to a purely vertical path by the machine rail.\", \"starting_position\": \"Stand with the bar resting across the upper trapezius, feet placed several centimeters anterior to the bar's vertical track, torso upright, knees soft, and the bar unracked by rotating it off the hooks.\", \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the knees can no longer track forward through the intended range without the hips shifting posteriorly to compensate, the heels lifting off the floor, or the lumbar spine rounding to complete the ascent.\", \"primary_joint_actions\": \"Knee extension is the dominant concentric action, supported by hip extension and ankle plantarflexion; the lumbar spine remains in a relatively fixed neutral position throughout since the fixed bar path removes the need for active anteroposterior trunk stabilization.\"}" |120|Roman Chair Back Extension               |"{\"grip\": \"\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Drive the movement from hip extension, not from arching the lower back past neutral.\", \"setup\": \"Hips pinned against the pad with the pelvis just above its top edge, ankles locked under the rear rollers, torso hanging in a straight line from hips to head.\", \"execution\": \"Extend the hips to bring the torso up to a straight line with the legs, then hinge forward again by folding at the hips while keeping the spine in one piece.\", \"stop_when\": \"The lumbar spine begins to round at the bottom or hyperextend past neutral at the top to complete the repetition.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet together or hip-width apart under the ankle pads, knees softly extended or very slightly flexed and held constant throughout the set.\", \"bracing\": \"Abdominal wall braced to lock the ribcage over the pelvis so the spine moves as a single unit; the lumbar curve is set once at the start and maintained through the full range rather than being actively flexed or extended segment by segment.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standard 45-degree Roman chair (hyperextension bench) back extension performed with bodyweight only, pelvis pivoting over the pad and torso moving between a forward-flexed hip position and a straight hip-to-head line. This distinguishes it from a lumbar-flexion/extension style hyperextension where the spine itself is allowed to round and arch through the range.\", \"eccentric\": \"Lower the torso back down by flexing at the hips under control, allowing the trunk to fold forward while the spine stays rigid, stopping once the torso is roughly parallel to the floor or where hip flexion range allows without spinal rounding.\", \"concentric\": \"Extend the hips to lift the torso upward, driving through the glutes and hamstrings until the body forms a straight line from ankles through hips to head; |128|Barbell Front Squat                      |"{\"grip\": \"Clean grip: fingertips hook the bar just outside shoulder width with wrists extended and elbows driven high; alternatively, a crossed-arm grip may be used, with each hand gripping the opposite shoulder of the bar to help pin it in place. In both variants the primary support for the bar comes from the elevated elbows and shoulder shelf, not from the hands.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the elbows driving upward and forward throughout the descent so the torso stays vertical and the bar stays over the midfoot.\", \"setup\": \"Bar rests across the anterior deltoids and clavicles, supported by an elevated-elbow front rack with fingertip or crossed-arm grip.\", \"execution\": \"Squat by flexing hips and knees simultaneously while keeping the torso upright and elbows lifted, then drive back up through the same path.\", \"stop_when\": \"The elbows drop and the torso pitches forward, causing the bar to roll off the shoulders or the lifter to lose the upright trunk position.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet approximately shoulder-width to slightly wider, toes turned out moderately to allow the knees to track in line with the toes through the full range.\", \"bracing\": \"Full abdominal brace with the ribcage held down over the pelvis before descending; the elevated elbow position must be actively maintained through upper-back and thoracic extension rather than relying solely on grip tension.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standard barbell front squat performed with the bar held in a front-rack position across the anterior deltoids, using either a clean (fingertip) grip or a crossed-arm grip. The anterior bar placement forces a more upright torso and greater knee travel relative to a back squat, shifting mechanical demand toward the quadriceps while requiring substantial thoracic and upper-back stabilization to keep the elbows elevated. This description assumes a standard depth-to-parallel-or-below squat performed for full repetitions, not a paused or tempo variant.\", \"eccentric\": \"Descend by flexing the hips and knees simultaneously, allowing the knees to travel forward over the toes while keeping the torso upright; the bar path should remain vertical over the midfoot, mirroring the ascent path in reverse.\", \"concentric\": \"Drive upward by extending the hips and knees together, keeping the torso angle relatively constant and the elbows lifted so the bar path travels in a vertical line over the midfoot. The chest should not collapse forward at any point during the ascent.\", \"tempo_notes\": \"Descent is controlled without bouncing at the bottom; a brief transition at depth is acceptable but should not involve relaxing the elevated elbow position or losing bar contact.\", \"end_position\": \"Standing with hips and knees fully extended, torso upright, and the bar still supported in the same front-rack position as the start.\", \"safety_notes\": [\"Ensure the barbell is secured against the shoulders with elevated elbows before initiating the descent to prevent it rolling forward mid-rep.\", \"Use safety pins or an appropriate rack height so the bar can be dumped safely if the front-rack position is lost.\", \"Avoid forcing wrist extension beyond a comfortable range when using the clean grip; the crossed-arm grip is an acceptable substitute for limited wrist mobility.\"], \"external_cues\": \"Keep the bar traveling straight up and down over the middle of the foot; imagine holding the elbows toward the ceiling throughout the movement.\", \"internal_cues\": \"Keep the elbows pointing forward and up; push the knees out in line with the toes; keep the ribcage stacked over the pelvis rather than flaring the chest upward.\", \"common_mistakes\": [\"Elbows dropping during the descent, causing the bar to roll forward off the shoulders.\", \"Excessive forward torso lean that shifts load away from the intended upright squat pattern.\", \"Knees collapsing inward during the ascent from the bottom position.\", \"Rising with the hips before the shoulders, flattening the torso angle prematurely.\", \"Cutting depth short as fatigue increases rather than maintaining the intended range of motion.\"], \"equipment_setup\": \"Bar positioned on a rack at approximately upper-chest to clavicle height so it can be unracked directly into the front-rack position without excessive shoulder elevation.\", \"range_of_motion\": \"Descend until the hip crease reaches or passes the level of the knee (at or below parallel), limited by the ability to maintain an upright torso and elevated elbows without the bar rolling forward; depth should not be forced past the point where the pelvis tucks under or the torso pitches forward.\", \"rir_0_definition\": \"Inability to complete another repetition while keeping the elbows elevated and the torso upright through full depth, even if the bar could still be moved using forward trunk lean or loss of the front-rack position.\", \"rir_1_indicators\": \"Noticeably slower ascent, brief hesitation out of the bottom position, and slight forward drift of the elbows that is still recoverable without losing bar position or upright torso.\", \"individualization\": \"Grip style (fingertip clean grip versus crossed-arm grip) may be selected based on wrist and shoulder mobility without changing the exercise identity, provided the elbows remain elevated and the bar stays supported on the shoulder shelf. Stance width and toe angle may vary moderately with hip structure as long as the knees track in line with the toes throughout the range. Squat depth may vary slightly with individual hip and ankle mobility, provided the torso remains upright and the elbows stay elevated throughout the repetition.\", \"plane_of_movement\": \"Primarily sagittal-plane hip and knee flexion/extension with the trunk maintained in a near-vertical orientation; minor frontal-plane control is required at the hips and knees to prevent valgus or lateral shift.\", \"starting_position\": \"Bar rests across the anterior deltoids and clavicles, contacting the throat area minimally; elbows are raised so the upper arms are close to parallel with the floor, keeping the humerus high enough that the bar does not roll forward. |134|Dumbbell Walking Lunge                   |"{\"grip\": \"Neutral (palms facing the body), dumbbells hanging freely; grip is functional only for holding the load and does not influence the lunge mechanics.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the front shin close to vertical at the bottom and drive through the front heel to stand up out of each rep.\", \"setup\": \"Stand upright holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with arms straight and shoulders relaxed.\", \"execution\": \"Step forward into a lunge, drop the rear knee toward the floor, then drive through the front leg to bring the rear foot forward into the next lunge, continuing in a walking pattern.\", \"stop_when\": \"You can no longer control the descent of the rear knee or the front knee drifts sharply inward/forward without the torso remaining upright.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet begin hip-width apart; each step lands with a stride length that allows the front shin to remain close to vertical at the bottom of the lunge, typically longer than a stationary lunge stride to accommodate forward travel.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain a neutral spine with the ribcage stacked over the pelvis throughout each step; avoid lateral trunk lean toward the working leg and avoid rotating the shoulders as the rear leg passes forward.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standard bilateral dumbbell walking lunge: dumbbells are held at the sides in a neutral grip (farmer/suitcase-style), and the lifter travels forward continuously by alternating stepping legs rather than returning to the start position after each repetition. The continuous forward-traveling pattern places sustained emphasis on single-leg deceleration and re-acceleration through the quadriceps and gluteus maximus.\", \"eccentric\": \"Step forward with one \"technical_failure\": \"The point at which the front knee can no longer be controlled through its full path (e.g., collapses inward, or the rear knee cannot be lowered under control), the torso approaches the chest.\", \"starting_position\": \"Sit with the torso upright or tilted back only 5–10 degrees from vertical, feet flat on the floor or footplate, arms fully extended overhead with the |183|Barbell Shrug                            |"{\"grip\": \"Pronated grip, hands set approximately shoulder-width to slightly outside shoulder-width, wrists kept straight to transmit force directly into the shoulder girdle without wrist flexion or extension.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Drive the scapulae straight up, not backward or forward.\", \"setup\": \"Stand upright holding a barbell at arm's length in front of the thighs with a shoulder-width or slightly wider pronated grip.\", \"execution\": \"Elevate the shoulder girdle straight upward toward the ears, then lower under control; the elbows and torso remain static throughout.\", \"stop_when\": \"You can no longer achieve full scapular elevation without recruiting elbow flexion or torso momentum to heave the bar upward.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet shoulder-width apart, knees soft but not actively flexing, weight balanced evenly over the midfoot.\", \"bracing\": \"Maintain a neutral spine with the ribcage aligned over the pelvis and abdominal wall lightly braced to prevent the torso from swaying or extending as the bar is lifted; the hips and knees remain still throughout.\", \"overview\": \"This is the standing barbell shrug, a scapular-elevation exercise performed with the bar held at arm's length using a straight, static grip. |173|Dumbbell Curl                            |"{\"grip\": \"Fully supinated grip (palms facing anteriorly) maintained from the bottom to the top of the repetition; grip width is set naturally by hand position at the sides and does not change during the set.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the upper arm pinned to the torso and let only the elbow joint move.\", \"setup\": \"Stand upright holding a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing forward (fully supinated) and arms hanging at the sides.\", \"execution\": \"Flex one elbow to curl the dumbbell in an arc toward the shoulder while the opposite arm stays extended, alternating sides each repetition.\", \"stop_when\": \"The working arm can no longer flex without the torso leaning back or the elbow drifting forward off the ribcage.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet approximately shoulder-width apart, knees soft, weight balanced evenly; a slight staggered stance is acceptable if it improves stability.\", \"bracing\": \"Abdominals and obliques braced to prevent lumbar hyperextension or trunk rocking; glutes lightly engaged to stabilize the pelvis; the non-working arm stays passively extended rather than swinging for momentum.\", \"overview\": \"This variant is a standing, free-weight biceps curl performed with a fixed supinated (palm-forward) grip maintained throughout the entire repetition, distinguishing it from hammer curls (neutral grip) and Zottman or rotating curls (grip changes during the movement). |181|Dumbbell Skull Crusher                   |"{\"grip\": \"Neutral or semi-neutral grip with palms facing each other or angled slightly inward; wrists held in a neutral, slightly extended position to keep the dumbbell load aligned over the forearm.\", \"tldr\": {\"focus\": \"Keep the upper arms perpendicular to the bench and motionless; all movement occurs at the elbow.\", \"setup\": \"Lie supine on a flat bench with both dumbbells pressed to lockout above the shoulders, upper arms vertical and fixed.\", \"execution\": \"Flex only the elbows to lower the dumbbells toward the forehead/temple area, then extend the elbows to return to lockout, keeping the upper arms stationary throughout.\", \"stop_when\": \"The upper arms begin to drift backward toward the face or the elbows flare outward to complete the lockout.\"}, \"stance\": \"Feet flat on the floor, shoulder-width apart, providing a stable base; hips remain on the bench throughout.\", \"bracing\": \"Scapulae pinned in retraction against the bench, ribcage kept down to avoid arching, and upper arms actively held vertical by the shoulder musculature so that only the forearms travel.\", \"overview\": \"This is the bilateral dumbbell skull crusher performed on a flat bench: both dumbbells are lowered simultaneously from an overhead lockout toward the forehead/temple region using elbow flexion only, with the upper arms held vertical throughout. It also differs from the 'lying triceps extension behind the head' variant, in which the dumbbells travel past the forehead toward the crown of the head with a greater degree of shoulder flexion; here the upper arm angle relative to the torso stays essentially constant near vertical.\", \"eccentric\": \"Allow the elbows to flex under control, lowering the dumbbells along the same arc toward the forehead/temple region while the upper arms remain fixed in their vertical position;
